# YYYMethods

## Study design

- Parallel RCT
- Study type: prevention
- Study duration: 5 May 2015 to 2 February 2019
- Study follow-up period: 60 days
- Diagnostic criteria of AKI: KDIGO
- Country: France
- Setting: multicentre ICU (3 sites)

# YYYParticipants

## Study characteristics

- Inclusion criteria: ≥ 18 years; receiving endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation during their stay in the ICU; weight increase of at least 3% during the stay; FiO2 ≤ 60%, PEEP ≤ 10 cm H20; no administration of catecholamines other than dobutamine at a dose of 10 µg/Kg/min
- Exclusion criteria: pregnancy; moribund state at ICU arrival; acute brain injury (traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage, intra-cerebral bleeding, stroke, meningo-encephalitis, coma from medication origin); CKD (CrCl < 30 mL/min/ and/or with chronic dialysis; mandatory administration of diuretics (cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, LVEF < 30%)

## Baseline characteristics

- Number: intervention group (89); control group (77)
- Median age, IQR (years): intervention group (66, 60 to 74); control group (66, 58 to 72)
- Male sex: intervention group (61); control group (61)

# YYYInterventions

## Intervention group

- Furosemide: once or twice a day until successful extubation. The dosage was adopted by the bedside physician with the aim of reaching the patient’s reference weight, with a maximum daily dose set at 250 mg of furosemide to avoid kidney toxicity. The administration of diuretics was postponed if one of the following criteria was present: urea > 25 mmol/L, creatinine > 180 μmol/L, CrCl ≤ 30 mL/min, administration of iodinated contrast product in the past 6 hours, natraemia > 150 mmol/L, kalaemia < 3 mmol/L, pH > 7.50, bicarbonates > 40 mmol/L. Once these metabolic issues were corrected, diuretics could be administered. After successful extubation, diuretic management was left to the attending physician’s discretion

## Control group

- Diuretic administration was prohibited. Diuretics could be used as rescue therapy in case of acute pulmonary oedema or de novo HF

# YYYOutcomes

## Reported outcomes

- Incidence of AKI
- Any use of KRT
- Death
- Adverse effects attributed to interventions (arrhythmias, hypokalaemia)
- Hyponatraemia ≤135 mmol/L
- Hypernatraemia ≥ 145 mmol/L
- Ventilatory free days
- In-ICU length of stay
- In-ICU death

characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Rehabilitation (Strategy 1, S1) (n = 59)

"The team of two trained nurses (see notes) applied one of the two rehabilitation strategies to each patient, beginning 72 hours after initial hospitalisation, when the patient’s clinical condition had been stabilised"

"The first strategy (S1) included two parts: education and physiotherapy. The education portion consisted of providing information on general care such as feeding, hygiene and mobilisation through a Manual of Physical Rehabilitation for the patient with Stroke and also verbally and through a practical rehabilitation training session provided by the nurse to the caregiver. This was an individual plan of daily rehabilitation according to the stage of Brunnstrom’s classification that the caregiver had to perform. The Manual was drafted by the research group, especially for this study. The physiotherapy part of the strategy was designed and applied based on the basal condition of the patients and their stage of physical recovery. The latter was defined using the Brunnstrom scale (I–III), which reflects voluntary activity, movement, coordination, postural stability, muscular tonicity and sphincter control (further details supplied in Table 1). The physiotherapy provided by nurse was divided into three phases. The intensive phase consisted of daily physical therapy initiated at the hospital and continued for two weeks postdischarge through in-home visits. The intermediate phase consisted of bi-weekly in-home visits during the following two weeks (weeks three and four postdischarge). Finally, the support phase consisted of weekly in-home visits during the following three months, up to four months postdischarge."

Length of intervention period: 4 months

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "average number of visits for the S1 group was 15 and the average duration of each visit had to be about 90 minutes"

Intervention provider: nurse (see notes) and caregiver

(2) No physical rehabilitation (Strategy two, S2) (n = 51)

"The second strategy (S2) consisted of education alone. The information and individual plan of rehabilitation provided by the nurse to the patient and caregiver were the same as in the S1 group. This intervention also began at the hospital and was continued in-home with weekly visits"

Length of intervention period: 4 months

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "The average number of visits in this group was eight and the average duration of each visit was approximately 45 minutes"

Intervention provider: nurse and caregiver

Study aim: "to evaluate the effectiveness of the early rehabilitation at hospital and its continuity at home provided by nurses, on the functional recovery of basic and social activities in stroke patients compared with conventional care" Torres-Arreola 2009

Design: parallel-group RCT

Country: Mexico

Study recruitment and setting: see Table 7

Involvement of patients/public/professionals/others: no

# YYYParticipants

Study population (number randomised): 110

Inclusion criteria:

- Age 40 years+

- Diagnosis of first stroke

- Ischaemic stroke

- Mild and moderate neurological damage

Exclusion criteria:

- Not reported

Participants: detailed in Table 28

PROGRESS-plus: summarised in Table 10

# YYYInterventions

(1) Rehabilitation (Strategy 1, S1) (n = 59)

"The team of two trained nurses (see notes) applied one of the two rehabilitation strategies to each patient, beginning 72 hours after initial hospitalisation, when the patient’s clinical condition had been stabilised"

"The first strategy (S1) included two parts: education and physiotherapy. The education portion consisted of providing information on general care such as feeding, hygiene and mobilisation through a Manual of Physical Rehabilitation for the patient with Stroke and also verbally and through a practical rehabilitation training session provided by the nurse to the caregiver. This was an individual plan of daily rehabilitation according to the stage of Brunnstrom’s classification that the caregiver had to perform. The Manual was drafted by the research group, especially for this study. The physiotherapy part of the strategy was designed and applied based on the basal condition of the patients and their stage of physical recovery. The latter was defined using the Brunnstrom scale (I–III), which reflects voluntary activity, movement, coordination, postural stability, muscular tonicity and sphincter control (further details supplied in Table 1). The physiotherapy provided by nurse was divided into three phases. The intensive phase consisted of daily physical therapy initiated at the hospital and continued for two weeks postdischarge through in-home visits. The intermediate phase consisted of bi-weekly in-home visits during the following two weeks (weeks three and four postdischarge). Finally, the support phase consisted of weekly in-home visits during the following three months, up to four months postdischarge."

Length of intervention period: 4 months

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "average number of visits for the S1 group was 15 and the average duration of each visit had to be about 90 minutes"

Intervention provider: nurse (see notes) and caregiver

(2) No physical rehabilitation (Strategy two, S2) (n = 51)

"The second strategy (S2) consisted of education alone. The information and individual plan of rehabilitation provided by the nurse to the patient and caregiver were the same as in the S1 group. This intervention also began at the hospital and was continued in-home with weekly visits"

Length of intervention period: 4 months

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "The average number of visits in this group was eight and the average duration of each visit was approximately 45 minutes"

Intervention provider: nurse and caregiver

# YYYOutcomes

Independence in ADL scales: Barthel Index

Motor function scales: NR

Measures of balance: NR

Measures of gait velocity: NR

Length of stay: NR

Adverse events: NR

Other measures: Frenchay Activities Index, MMSE, Canadian Neurological Scale

Time points when outcomes were assessed: "Before randomisation, the patient and/or relatives were interviewed in the hospital to evaluate the patient’s basic ADL (Barthel index) and social activities (Frenchay index), which were used as the main outcome variables"

"Follow-up measurements of the basic and social ADL and the cognitive state of the stroke patient were obtained at one, three and six months postdischarge"

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

Randomized, parallel, open-label design

# YYYParticipants

172 patients on warfarin for more than one week and planning to remain on this drug for at least one month after elective implantation of a pacemaker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator.

# YYYInterventions

Half dose of warfarin for 3–6 days, depending on the baseline international normalized ratio (INR), before surgery aiming at an INR of ≤ 1.7 was compared with interrupted warfarin for 5 days with preoperative bridging with low-molecular-weight heparin at therapeutic dose for 2.5 days.

# YYYOutcomes

Primary outcomes: pocket hematoma, severe pocket hematoma.

Secondary outcomes were major bleeding, arterial or venous thromboembolism, death, length of hospitalization and reversal with vitamin K on the day before surgery to achieve an INR of ≤ 1.7.

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

* Study design: 3-arm parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: multi-centre (Copenhagen University Hospital—Rigshospitalet, Aarhus University Hospital, and University Hospital of Southern Denmark—Vejle Hospital)

* Number randomised: 97 children

* Study follow-up: 3 years

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: 3 (3.1%) were lost to follow-up by 12 months

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 9.4 years (range 6-12 years)

* Gender: 42 boys, 55 girls

* Culture: Danish

* Inclusion criteria:

* age 6 to 12 years
* myopia (SER by cycloplegic autorefraction in at least one eye) of ≥1 D if age was ≥6 to <9 years, or ≥2 D if age was ≥9 to ≤12 years; and astigmatism of <1.5 D
* Exclusion criteria:

* ocular pathology (e.g. amblyopia, strabismus, and keratoconus)
* myopia related to retinal dystrophies, connective tissue disorders (e.g. Ehlers Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and Sticklers syndrome), previous eye surgery
* previous use of agents thought to affect myopia progression (e.g. atropine, pirenzepine or 7-methylxanthine)
* previous use of soft bifocal/multifocal or orthokeratology contact lenses
* known allergy to atropine or any of the contents of the trial medication, non-compliance to eye examinations
* serious systemic health troubles (e.g. cardiac or respiratory illness), and developmental disorders and delays

# YYYInterventions

* 0.01% atropine eyedrops (n = 32)

* 0.1% loading dose for 6 months followed by 0.01% for 6 months (N=33)

* Placebo (n = 32)

# YYYOutcomes

* Primary outcome

* Change in AL at 12 months, measured by a swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT)-based biometer
* Secondary outcome

* Change in SER at 12 months, measured by cycloplegic autorefraction
* Measurements taken at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24 (treatment stop and washout start), 30, and 36 months

* Unit of analysis: participant (average of both eyes)

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Randomisation process** | Low risk of bias | Randomisation was performed using a randomisation instrument in Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap). Allocation was appropriately concealed using sealed envelopes. Baseline differences did not suggest a problem with the randomisation process. |
| **Deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk of bias | Participants, care providers, investigators, and outcome assessors were masked. Analysis followed ITT principles. |
| **Missing outcome data** | Low risk of bias | Data available for nearly all (97%) of participants. |
| **Measurement of the outcome** | Low risk of bias | Appropriate and comparable methods of measuring outcome data were used. Outcome assessors were masked. Therefore, it is unlikely that the outcome was influenced by knowledge of the intervention received. |
| **Selection of the reported results** | Some concerns | Trial registry entry is available, but insufficient information (e.g. SAP) to judge this domain. |
| **Overall** | Some concerns | The study is judged to raise some concerns in at least one domain for this result, but not to be at high risk of bias for any domain. |

characteristics_interventions.S:
## General details

* **Surgeon:** Not reported

* **Components:** Cobalt chrome alloy stem, bipolar head, 41 press-fit, 2 cemented stem

* **Anaesthesia:** Not reported

* **Care protocol:** After admission, patients were actively treated for comorbidities, underwent preoperative preparation, and received preoperative education. Once the preoperative preparation was completed, the surgery was scheduled. Both procedures were performed with the patient in a standard lateral position. There were no specific positioning requirements for the SuperPATH group. However, for the anterolateral group, special restrictions were applied: "D-shaped shoe," internal rotation of the lower limbs, and abduction. When lying on the unaffected side, a pillow was placed between the legs to prevent adduction and external rotation of the lower limb. Both groups received prophylactic anticoagulant medication, using rivaroxaban, which continued as part of their ongoing treatment. After the anaesthesia wore off, active movement was encouraged. For the SuperPATH group, patients were encouraged to walk with the assistance of a walking aid or crutches on the second day after surgery, without any specific range of motion restrictions. For the anterolateral group, patients were allowed to walk on the ground after one week, with toes pointing forward. They were instructed to avoid hip flexion exceeding 90°, external rotation of the affected limb, and crossing their legs for six months. Regular follow-up examinations were scheduled at 3 and 6 months postoperatively, and then annually.

## Intervention group 1 (Posterior)

"Conventional Instrumentation SuperPATH Approach (Experimental Group) [5-7]: The hip joint was flexed to approximately 60°, internally rotated by 20°, and slightly adducted. Along the axis of the femur, a longitudinal incision was made starting approximately 2 cm below the tip of the greater trochanter, extending proximally for about 8 cm. The gluteus maximus muscle was bluntly separated and retracted to expose the gluteus medius muscle. Instead of using the specialised retractor for SuperPATH technique, a conventional "S" hook was used to retract the gluteus medius muscle anteriorly, revealing the piriformis muscle and the gluteus minimus muscle. At this point, unnamed vessels crossing the surgical field were often visible, and electrocoagulation was performed to control bleeding and avoid interference with the surgical process. Access was gained through the gap between the piriformis and gluteus minimus muscles, entering the joint capsule beneath. The capsule could be incised in a "T" or "L" shape, revealing the femoral neck and acetabulum, as well as the intertrochanteric fossa and the apex of the greater trochanter. Two commonly used acetabular hooks were used instead of the specialised blunt hook for SuperPATH, inserted along the anterior and posterior aspects of the femoral neck cortex, allowing simultaneous retraction of the joint capsule and surrounding muscle groups, resulting in good exposure of the surgical field. Under direct visualization, fracture reduction could usually be easily achieved, which helped determine the anteversion angle (or based on the residual axis of the fracture ends). A Kirschner wire could be used as a substitute for SuperPATH to determine the direction of the femoral medullary cavity."

## Intervention group 2 (Lateral)

"Conventional Instrumentation Anterolateral Approach (Control Group) [8]: A modified Hardinge approach was used, where the iliotibial tract was bluntly separated, and the gluteus medius muscle was retracted. The anterior one-third of the gluteus medius muscle and the gluteus minimus muscle were cut near their insertions, and the retracted muscles were then mobilized inward. This provided good exposure to the anterior aspect of the joint capsule, which was then excised. The femoral neck was preserved approximately 1.0 cm, and osteotomy was performed to remove the femoral head. The diameter was measured, and an appropriate femoral head was selected. The femoral side was opened, the medullary canal was reamed distally, and the proximal portion was shaped. After successful completion, the joint was irrigated, and the prosthesis was implanted. In the case of a cemented prosthesis, a medullary canal plug was placed, followed by insertion of an exhaust tube. After injecting bone cement, the exhaust tube was removed, and the femoral stem containing the intermediate component was inserted, ensuring no overflow. After solidification, neck length was checked, and the dual articulation head was installed. Finally, reduction was performed, and the joint was tested for movement in all directions without impingement, stable and not dislocating, with good tension. Extensive irrigation was performed, and approximately 50 mL of tranexamic acid solution was injected into the surrounding soft tissues to reduce bleeding. After confirming no active bleeding, the joint capsule was sutured and repaired, and the decision to place a drain was based on the presence of exudate. The incision was closed."

# YYYMethods

Aim: non-inferiority, efficacy and safety
Design: parallel-group/dose-escalation (phase II)
Blinding: double-blind, double-dummy; groups blinded: participants, outcome adjudicators
Study duration: December 2003 to April 2005
Duration of intervention: 6 to 10 days
Duration of follow-up: 22 ± 7 days
Method of randomisation: stratified by type of surgery (THR/TKR); no additional description provided
Method of concealment of allocation: not mentioned
Primary efficacy analysis set: participants who: 1) received at least one dose of study medication, 2) un-
derwent planned surgery, 3) had a primary efficacy outcome that could be evaluated, 4) had no proto-
col violations that could potentially impact on efficacy evaluation (per-protocol population)
Primary safety analysis set: participants who received at least one dose of study medication
Withdrawals: not reported
Exclusions: LY517717 groups (not detailed according to dose group): 3 did not receive study drug; 8 did
not undergo planned surgery; 91 were not evaluable for any VTE event, 41 did not undergo venography,
50 had uninterpretable venography (not further detailed); 24 had major protocol violations (3 received
< 5 doses of study drug, 9 used excluded intervention, 3 violated study drug tasting requirement, 9 oth-
er). Enoxaparin group: 1 did not receive study drug; 2 did not undergo planned surgery; 16 were not
evaluable for any VTE event, 12 did not undergo venography, 4 had uninterpretable venography (not
further detailed); 6 had major protocol violations (0 received < 5 doses of study drug, 2 used excluded
intervention, 3 violated study drug tasting requirement, 1 other)

* Study design: parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: single (Eye Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, Wenzhou, China)

* Number randomised: 170 children

* Study follow-up: 2 years

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: 9 (5%) were excluded or lost to follow-up

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 10.4 years (range 8-13 years)

* Gender: 73 boys, 88 girls

* Culture: Chinese

* Inclusion criteria:

* cycloplegic SER between −0.75 D and −4.75 D
* astigmatism of cycloplegic autorefraction not exceeding 1.50 D
* anisometropia not exceeding 1.00 D based on SER
* monocular best corrected VA of 0.05 logMAR or better at distance for both eyes
* absence of ocular pathology
* absence of binocular vision issues and no history of ocular surgery or use of myopia control measures
* Exclusion criteria:

* history of PALs or BF use and no prior use of contact lenses
* strabismus by cover test at near and distance
* ocular or systemic medicine, which might affect myopia progression or VA through known effects on retina, accommodation or significant elevation of IOP

# YYYInterventions

* HAL n = 58
* SAL n = 57
* SVL n = 55

* Primary outcomes

* Change in SER error from baseline (cycloplegic autorefraction)
* Change in AL from baseline (Topcon KR-800)
* Secondary outcomes

* Distance and near BCVA (ETDRS Chart)
* Time needed to adapt to the lenses
* Compliance (self-reported daily wearing hours)
* AEs
* Measurements at 6-monthly intervals for 24 months

* Unit of analysis: data from right eye analysed

* **Location:** Spain, 4 centres

  * Number randomised: unclear

## Participant (baseline) characteristics

* Age: 42.23 (SD 13.92) years
* Gender (F/M): 140 (45.5%)/168 (54.5%)
* Main diagnosis: CSOM (purulent discharge for > 3 months and perforated tympanic membrane)
* High-risk population

  * Cleft palate (or other craniofacial malformation): not reported
  * Down's syndrome: not reported
  * Indigenous groups (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people/Greenland natives): not reported

  * Alternative diagnosis of ear discharge: not reported
  * Number who have previously had grommets inserted: not reported
  * Number who have had previous ear surgery: not reported
  * Number who had previous antibiotic treatment for CSOM: not reported, 0% in previous 48 hours (exclusion criteria)

* Adults aged 18–65 years
* Chronic otitis media in suppurative phase with purulent discharge for > 3 months with a perforated ear drum

* Cholesteatoma
* Pregnant/breastfeeding
* Severe renal or hepatic insufficiency
* Antibiotic treatment in previous 48 hours
* Bilateral hearing loss > 60 decibels

characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Task specific training (TST) combined with cognitive sensorimotor exercise (CSE)

"performed sense, trunk stability, lower-extremity movements, and gait training in a sitting or standing position by applying CSE and the TST. In this study, 30min of CSE and 30min of the TST were performed five times per week for eight weeks. Two physical therapists performed treatment to reduce treatment bias. One physical therapist with more than five years of clinical experience performed the CSE exercises. The TST training was conducted by the researcher who has more than 5 years of clinical experience. The participants were trained to recognize their bodies using visual and somatosensory techniques. The CSE consisted of proprioceptive training, tactile training, heel pressure, and space tasks. For CSE using a spatial task, exercise programs were given to distinguish distance and direction. The CSE was applied for a total of 30 min for 5min each with the subjects." Cognitive sensorimotor exercise program is detailed in table 1 - comprises of 5 minutes each of proprioceptive training, tactile stimulation training, pressure stimulation training, and two spatial tasks.

"The 30 min TST consisted of the following: 10 min of trunk stability and sit to stand training while controlling the movement trunk and lower extremities [25], 10 min of lower extremity movements and gait training while controlling scapular movement [26,27], 10 min of progressive body weight support treadmill training while controlling the movement of the lower extremities" (see note below about TST).

(2) Task specific training (TST) combined with conventional physical therapy

"The Experimental II group performed trunk stability and sit-to-stand training while controlling the movement of the trunk and lower extremities, lower extremity movements and gait training while controlling scapular movement, and progressive body weight support treadmill training while controlling the movement of the lower extremities. Experimental II group received 30 min of the TST and 30 min of conventional physical therapy five times per week for eight weeks."

NOTE: in the trials registry, this (TST) intervention is described as "Bobath therapy motor program". Stating that this: "targets trunk stabilisation and the sit-to-stand motion, lower extremity movement and gain training, and progressive body weight support treadmill training".

(3) Conventional physical therapy

"The conservative physical therapy program consisted of ROM exercises, stretching exercises, upper- and lower-extremity muscle strengthening exercise, ground gait training, bike exercises, balance training, and superdynamics exercises. The control group received conservative physical 30 min twice daily, five times per week for 8 weeks."

# YYYMethods

Study aim: examine the effects of task-specific training combined with cognitive sensorimotor exercise on proprioception, spasticity and gait speed in people with stroke

Design: multi-arm RCT (3 arms)

Country: Korea, Rep.

Study recruitment and setting: see Table 7

Involvement of patients/public/professionals/others: no

# YYYParticipants

Study population (number randomised): 45

Inclusion criteria:

- Diagnosis of stroke with onset of ≥ 6 months

- Able to walk at least 10 m

- MMSE-Korean version ≥ 24

- Able to communicate and follow the instructions

- Brunnstrom exercise recovery stages of 3–4 or higher

- No problem walking due to ankle joint contractures

- No sensory deficiencies of the lower extremities

- Able to provide informed consent

Exclusion criteria:

- Vestibular problems

- Cerebellar-related diseases

- Visual or hearing impairments;

- Unable to participate due to severe cognitive decline or aphasia

- Unilateral neglect

Participants: detailed in Table 28

# YYYInterventions

(1) Task specific training (TST) combined with cognitive sensorimotor exercise (CSE)

"performed sense, trunk stability, lower-extremity movements, and gait training in a sitting or standing position by applying CSE and the TST. In this study, 30min of CSE and 30min of the TST were performed five times per week for eight weeks. Two physical therapists performed treatment to reduce treatment bias. One physical therapist with more than five years of clinical experience performed the CSE exercises. The TST training was conducted by the researcher who has more than 5 years of clinical experience. The participants were trained to recognize their bodies using visual and somatosensory techniques. The CSE consisted of proprioceptive training, tactile training, heel pressure, and space tasks. For CSE using a spatial task, exercise programs were given to distinguish distance and direction. The CSE was applied for a total of 30 min for 5min each with the subjects." Cognitive sensorimotor exercise program is detailed in table 1 - comprises of 5 minutes each of proprioceptive training, tactile stimulation training, pressure stimulation training, and two spatial tasks.

"The 30 min TST consisted of the following: 10 min of trunk stability and sit to stand training while controlling the movement trunk and lower extremities [25], 10 min of lower extremity movements and gait training while controlling scapular movement [26,27], 10 min of progressive body weight support treadmill training while controlling the movement of the lower extremities" (see note below about TST).

(2) Task specific training (TST) combined with conventional physical therapy

"The Experimental II group performed trunk stability and sit-to-stand training while controlling the movement of the trunk and lower extremities, lower extremity movements and gait training while controlling scapular movement, and progressive body weight support treadmill training while controlling the movement of the lower extremities. Experimental II group received 30 min of the TST and 30 min of conventional physical therapy five times per week for eight weeks."

NOTE: in the trials registry, this (TST) intervention is described as "Bobath therapy motor program". Stating that this: "targets trunk stabilisation and the sit-to-stand motion, lower extremity movement and gain training, and progressive body weight support treadmill training".

(3) Conventional physical therapy

"The conservative physical therapy program consisted of ROM exercises, stretching exercises, upper- and lower-extremity muscle strengthening exercise, ground gait training, bike exercises, balance training, and superdynamics exercises. characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Group therapy task training

"Patients assigned to the experimental group received a 90-minute, structured progressive task training program five times a week over a six week period (30 sessions). Each training included eight out of ten available work stations, intended to improve tasks relating to walking competency, such as balance control, stair walking, turning, transfers and speed walking. Graded progression was achieved by (1) increasing the difficulty of the task, (2) adding weights, or (3) increasing the number of repetitions. At each work station, participants worked together in pairs: while one participant performed the task for three minutes, the other one observed him and counted the number of repetitions. After three minutes of practice or observation, they reversed roles. After six minutes at one work station, each pair had one minute to go to the next work station."

"The total group training program included four stages: warming up (10 minutes), task training (60 minutes), sports and games (15 minutes) and cooling down (5 minutes)."

(2) Individual task training

"Patients allocated to the individual training received a 90-minute, progressive individually tailored task training 5 times a week over a 6 week period (30 sessions) offered by one of the staff physical therapists. The training was tailored to the deficits of the patient and aimed to improve balance, physical condition and walking competency, preferably using a graded progression"

"Both interventions lasted six weeks and were given during in-patient rehabilitation, the broad aim of both types of intervention was to improve the patients’ mobility to allow safe discharge to their homes. Both groups received all other therapies including neuropsychology, speech, and occupational therapy for the upper paretic limb, as needed."

Country: Germany

# YYYParticipants

Study population (number randomised): 73

Inclusion criteria:

- Verified stroke according to WHO confirmed by CT scan

- Able to sit and stand independently

- Able to walk with assistance (i.e. FAC # 2 and # 4) with or without an aid or orthosis

- Able to understand instructions (MMSE > 23)

Exclusion criteria:

- Lived > 70 km from rehabilitation centre

Participants: detailed in Table 28

PROGRESS-plus: summarised in Table 10

# YYYInterventions

(1) Group therapy task training

"Patients assigned to the experimental group received a 90-minute, structured progressive task training program five times a week over a six week period (30 sessions). Each training included eight out of ten available work stations, intended to improve tasks relating to walking competency, such as balance control, stair walking, turning, transfers and speed walking. Graded progression was achieved by (1) increasing the difficulty of the task, (2) adding weights, or (3) increasing the number of repetitions. At each work station, participants worked together in pairs: while one participant performed the task for three minutes, the other one observed him and counted the number of repetitions. After three minutes of practice or observation, they reversed roles. After six minutes at one work station, each pair had one minute to go to the next work station."

"The total group training program included four stages: warming up (10 minutes), task training (60 minutes), sports and games (15 minutes) and cooling down (5 minutes)."

(2) Individual task training

"Patients allocated to the individual training received a 90-minute, progressive individually tailored task training 5 times a week over a 6 week period (30 sessions) offered by one of the staff physical therapists. The training was tailored to the deficits of the patient and aimed to improve balance, physical condition and walking competency, preferably using a graded progression"

"Both interventions lasted six weeks and were given during in-patient rehabilitation, the broad aim of both types of intervention was to improve the patients’ mobility to allow safe discharge to their homes. Both groups received all other therapies including neuropsychology, speech, and occupational therapy for the upper paretic limb, as needed."

characteristics_interventions.S:
**Intervention**

Regionalisation of trauma services in England.

**Description of rationale, theory, or goal of essential elements to the intervention**

Trauma Audit and Research Network had identified significant variation in the standard of care in England, and comparative studies showed that the outcome following trauma did not meet the standards of other countries. Further, the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) 2007 report suggested that almost 60% of major trauma patients received a less than good practice standard, with avoidable deaths still occurring. This led the National audit office to recommend the development of regional trauma networks in England. There was system change and re-configuration in 2012 with 27 large hospitals to (MTC) operating within a network of smaller trauma units. After establishing trauma systems, there was a need to assess their impact on the healthcare system at the time of the study; there was still a controversy about the optimal way to organise health series for patients suffering severe injury.

**Description of providers (background, expertise, training)**

Not provided.

**Mode of delivery of the intervention (face-to-face, telephone, and Internet)**

Establish MTC and trauma networks (regionalisation). Trauma patients were retrieved from the scene and triaged to MTC based on shared ambulance protocols.

**Description of location(s) infrastructure or relevant features of where intervention occurred**

Re-configuration of all hospitals in England into comprehensive trauma networks. Additional funding was provided for severely injured patients whose care satisfied several inclusion criteria.

**How well was their intervention planned (if fidelity or adherence was assessed, describe how, by who, and if strategies for maintaining fidelity were employed)**

Limited descriptions of the physical infrastructure and how the intervention was implemented.

**How well was the intervention carried out, description of how the intervention adhered to the plan**

Not described.

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

| Characteristic    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Study design**  | Interrupted time series (ITS).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Study centres** | Over the study period, 98 hospitals joined the Trauma Audit & Research Network (TARN) for the first time, increasing membership from 91 hospitals in 2008/9 to 169 hospitals in 2016/17, including all designated major trauma centres (MTCs) and Trauma Units. they identified 35 hospitals with continuous TARN membership and patient submissions throughout the study period, and they defined these as 'consistent submitters' |
| **Study setting** | England                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Withdrawals**   | Not applicable (retrospective study)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Date of study** | April 2008 to March 2017                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Follow-up**     | 9 years follow-up                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

# YYYParticipants

| Characteristic            | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Number**                | 110863 from hospitals defined as 'consistent submitters' of data to TARN                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Age**                   | Median 45 (pre-intervention) and 59 (post-intervention)                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Sex**                   | Male 61-67%                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Severity of condition** | Median ISS16 in both periods                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Diagnostic criteria**   | Not described                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Inclusion criteria**    | All patients included within the TARN registry, which includes those sustaining a severe injury resulting in hospital admission > 72 hours, critical care admission, transfer to a tertiary/specialist centre or death within 30 days. |
| **Exclusion criteria**    | Patients with ISS <9 and those aged >65 with isolated femoral neck fractures                                                                                                                                                           |

# YYYInterventions

**Intervention**

Regionalisation of trauma services in England.

**Description of rationale, theory, or goal of essential elements to the intervention**

Trauma Audit and Research Network had identified significant variation in the standard of care in England, and comparative studies showed that the outcome following trauma did not meet the standards of other countries. Further, the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) 2007 report suggested that almost 60% of major trauma patients received a less than good practice standard, with avoidable deaths still occurring. This led the National audit office to recommend the development of regional trauma networks in England. There was system change and re-configuration in 2012 with 27 large hospitals to (MTC) operating within a network of smaller trauma units. After establishing trauma systems, there was a need to assess their impact on the healthcare system at the time of the study; there was still a controversy about the optimal way to organise health series for patients suffering severe injury.

**Description of providers (background, expertise, training)**

Not provided.

**Mode of delivery of the intervention (face-to-face, telephone, and Internet)**

Establish MTC and trauma networks (regionalisation). Trauma patients were retrieved from the scene and triaged to MTC based on shared ambulance protocols.

**Description of location(s) infrastructure or relevant features of where intervention occurred**

Re-configuration of all hospitals in England into comprehensive trauma networks. Additional funding was provided for severely injured patients whose care satisfied several inclusion criteria.

**How well was their intervention planned (if fidelity or adherence was assessed, describe how, by who, and if strategies for maintaining fidelity were employed)**

Limited descriptions of the physical infrastructure and how the intervention was implemented.

**How well was the intervention carried out, description of how the intervention adhered to the plan**

Not described.

# YYYOutcomes

Study outcomes were: trends of patient's characteristics, process of care and patient outcomes such as adjusted survival rate and mortality. these included, patient flow, the evolution of consultant-led care and imaging, increase in older age of trauma admission, and establishment of newer clinical care protocols (i.e., massive transfusion protocols and tranexamic acid protocols). There were 10247 (9.2%) deaths in the 110863 patients with an ISS of 9 or more.

There were no changes in unadjusted mortality. Risk-adjusted survival showed a 19% (95% CI 3%-36%) increase in the case-mix adjusted odds of survival in severe injury over the 9-year study period. Interrupted time series analysis showed a significant positive change in the slope after the intervention time point of April 2012 (+0.08% excess survivors per quarter, p = 0.023), i.e., an increase of 0.08 more survivors per 100 patients every quarter.

**Patient characteristic trends:** demography (age, sex etc.), injury severity (ISS), mechanism of injury (penetrating/blunt, falls) and comorbidities.

**Process of care:** time to arrival to ED, time to intubation at ED, Consultant led care at ED, time to Blood transfusion, time to surgery, percentage admitted to ICU, length of stay in hospital/ICU.

characteristics_outcomes.S:
Study outcomes were: trends of patient's characteristics, process of care and patient outcomes such as adjusted survival rate and mortality. these included, patient flow, the evolution of consultant-led care and imaging, increase in older age of trauma admission, and establishment of newer clinical care protocols (i.e., massive transfusion protocols and tranexamic acid protocols). There were 10247 (9.2%) deaths in the 110863 patients with an ISS of 9 or more.

There were no changes in unadjusted mortality. Risk-adjusted survival showed a 19% (95% CI 3%-36%) increase in the case-mix adjusted odds of survival in severe injury over the 9-year study period. Interrupted time series analysis showed a significant positive change in the slope after the intervention time point of April 2012 (+0.08% excess survivors per quarter, p = 0.023), i.e., an increase of 0.08 more survivors per 100 patients every quarter.

**Patient characteristic trends:** demography (age, sex etc.), injury severity (ISS), mechanism of injury (penetrating/blunt, falls) and comorbidities.

**Process of care:** time to arrival to ED, time to intubation at ED, Consultant led care at ED, time to Blood transfusion, time to surgery, percentage admitted to ICU, length of stay in hospital/ICU.

characteristics_interventions.S:
Caesarean myomectomy vs caesarean section alone.

* **Intervention:** Caesarean myomectomy. An IV infusion of 1000 mg tranexamic acid was done just before induction of anesthesia. A Foley's catheter was fixed in the urinary bladder and 400 mg misoprostol was inserted rectally just after induction of anesthesia. Following delivery of the fetus, the uterine artery was ligated bilaterally then a longitudinal linear uterine incision was performed to allow removal of the myoma by enucleation then the myoma cavity was closed by purse string suture and the overlying serosa was closed by continuous suture. The uterine transverse incision was then repaired, a wide pore drain was then inserted in the Douglas pouch, and the abdominal wall was repaired. Post surgery, another 400mg misoprostol was inserted rectally postoperatively and the oxytocin infusion was continued for 24 h.
* **Control:** Caesarean section

(1) Motor relearning group (n = 33)

"Both programmes were conducted in the same treatment area located in the occupational therapy department of the hospital. The patients in both programmes also received physical therapy in the form of lower limb strengthening and trunk balance exercises. The patients attended physical therapy from one to three times a week. Their attendance was monitored throughout the study, and the number of sessions was incorporated into the analysis of the results"

"In the motor relearning programme, the intervention technique followed four sequential steps: identification of the missing performance components (step 1), training using remedial exercises (step 2), training using functional task components (step 3), and transfer of skills to functional task performance (step 4). A total of 24 remedial tasks (used in step 2) and 10 functional tasks (used in step 4) were designed to cover deficits in static and dynamic sitting balance, and static and dynamic standing balance. Throughout the training session, the therapist stressed the importance of relating the training processes taking place in steps 2 and 3 to practices in step 4. The training progressed by advancing from a sitting to a standing position, and from static to dynamic balancing. The criteria established for progression were clearly defined, and those patients who demonstrated the desirable skills were upgraded to another stage of training"

Length of intervention period: 6 weeks

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: 3 x 2-hour sessions each week (18 sessions total) Chan DY 2006

Intervention provider: occupational therapist: "The researcher conducted the motor relearning programme"

(2) Skills training group (n = 33)

"The skill training method was adopted for use with patients receiving the conventional therapy programme. The same number of remedial and functional tasks was covered as in the motor relearning programme. The selection of remedial tasks followed the principle of progressing from a sitting to a standing position, and from static to dynamic balance. The training of functional tasks began with simple self-care and bedside tasks, such as bed mobility, and progressed to more complicated tasks, such as use of community facilities. Unlike the motor relearning programme, the patients were not involved in identifying their own missing performance components (Table 22). The relationships between the practices of the remedial tasks and the entire functional task performance were not reinforced"

Length of intervention period: 6 weeks

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: 3 x 2-hour sessions each week (18 sessions total)

Intervention provider: "another occupational therapist conducted the conventional therapy programme. The therapist responsible for the conventional therapy programme was trained in the standardized procedure for conducting the control programme"

Throughout the training session, the therapist stressed the importance of relating the training processes taking place in steps 2 and 3 to practices in step 4. The training progressed by advancing from a sitting to a standing position, and from static to dynamic balancing. * Study design: parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: single (Hospital of Yunnan University, China)

* Number randomized: 176 children

* Study follow-up: 3 years (24 months of treatment, 1 year withdrawal)

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: 34 were excluded or lost to follow-up at 36 m

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 9.19 (SD 0.77) years (range 7 to 12 years)

* Gender: 71 boys, 71 girls

* Culture: Chinese

* Inclusion criteria:

* myopic refraction range SER from -1.00 to -6.00 D
* 7 to 12 years old
* willing to participate in the 3-year clinical observation
* annual growth rate of SER ≥0.75 D/y before the investigation
* binocular vision was normal
* initial IOP<21 mm Hg
* tolerable to atropine eye drops.
* Exclusion criteria:

* history of allergies to atropine
* history of ocular organic diseases such as strabismus, amblyopia, congenital cataract and optic nerve dysplasia
* history of ocular surgeries
* history of systemic diseases that affected visual function, such as diabetes and chromosomal abnormalities
* history of use of contact lenses, bifocal or multifocal lenses, or other myopia treatments (such as pilocarpine)

# YYYInterventions

* 0.05% atropine (n=88)

* Placebo (n=88)

* Primary outcome

* Change in spherical equivalent cycloplegic autorefraction
* Secondary outcome

* Change in AL as measured by non contact partial coherence interferometry in the study eye
* Measurements taken at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months

* Unit of analysis: both eyes (generalised estimating equations model)

# YYYMethods

Study aim: to investigate the effects of body awareness therapy on balance, mobility, balance confidence, and subjective health status in persons with stroke

Design: parallel-group RCT

Country: Sweden

Study recruitment and setting: see Table 7

Involvement of patients/public/professionals/others: unclear

# YYYParticipants

Study population (number randomised): 46

Inclusion criteria:

- > 6 months since onset of the most recent stroke

- Able to walk a distance of 100 m with or without assistance

- Subjectively experienced balance impairment (i.e. a yes on the question ‘do you feel that your

balance is impaired?’)

Exclusion criteria:

- Medical, physical or cognitive impairment that affected the ability to actively participate or to

understand written and verbal instructions

Participants: detailed in Table 28

PROGRESS-plus: summarised in Table 10

(1) Body awareness therapy (n = 24)

"The experimental intervention was an add-on therapy to the participants’ usual daily activities"

"The experimental intervention consisted of body awareness therapy in groups for eight weeks, 60 minutes once a week. Four sessions was set as the minimum for participation in the intervention. The intervention was led by physiotherapists with further training and 15–20 years of clinical experience in body aware- Lindvall 2014 ness therapy. The choice of movements in the intervention was based on earlier body awareness therapy studies, and experiences from the physiotherapists responsible for the intervention. Unclear whether allocation concealment was performed or not. No group differences in baseline characteristics were reported. |
| **Deviations from intended interventions** | Some concerns | It was described as a double-blind trial. No information on method of analysis. Missingness unlikely to depend on true value. |
| **Missing outcome data** | High risk of bias | No information on losses to follow up. Insufficient information was provided to judge whether appopriate analysis was used. No flowchart was available. |
| **Measurement of the outcome** | Low risk of bias | The outcome was measured using objective clinical tests. It was unlikely that the measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between groups. # YYYMethods

* Study design: parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: single (Shenyang He Eye Specialist Hospital Co)

* Number randomised: 295 children

* Study follow-up: 12 months

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: not reported

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = Not reported (range 6-13 years)

* Gender: 148 boys, 147 girls

* Culture: Chinese

* Inclusion criteria:

* aged 6 to 13 years old
* myopia prevention and control needs
* binocular myopia spherical power -0.5 to -6.00D
* astigmatism ≤2.0D
* Exclusion criteria:

* other eye diseases, such as amblyopia, constant strabismus, acute keratoconjunctivitis, congenital glaucoma or other fundus diseases
* ocular and systemic lesions requiring local or systemic use of atropine or pyrazine drugs
* those who are allergic to atropine, or have systemic diseases (such as heart or respiratory diseases)
* those who have not received any treatment within 3 months before screening
* those who have used, are currently using, or plan to use other myopia prevention and control methods such as orthokeratology lenses, RGP, peripheral defocus, and progressive multifocal glasses during the study period
* other conditions that the researchers believe are not suitable for participation in this study.

* 0.01% atropine eyedrops (n=197)

* Placebo (n=98)

* Primary outcomes

* BCVA
* IOP
* Pupil diameter
* Accommodative amplitude
* Change in AL from baseline (measured by the NIDEK AL-Scan optical biometer)
* Change in SER from baseline (cycloplegic autorefraction)
* Adverse events
* Measurements taken at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months

* Unit of analysis: participant (right eye)

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

| Characteristic             | Description                |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| **Study design**           | RCT (cross-over)           |
| **Data-collection period** | October 2008 to March 2009 |

# YYYParticipants

* **Country:** Australia.
* Two mixed-gender long-term care facilities, which provided low care—assisted living—and high care—nursing home.
* **Participants:** 47; 33 women and 14 men.

## Dementia diagnosis

* Confirmed diagnosis of early- to mid-stage dementia; or
* probable dementia, defined as a cognitive impairment level of 12 to 24 on the MMSE; or
* AD according to DSM-IV criteria.

Participants had “a documented behavioural history of agitation/aggression on nursing/medical records within the last month.”

## Baseline characteristics

* Type of dementia was not reported.
* **Age:** 3 people aged 65 to 74 years; 13 aged 75 to 84 years; 28 aged 85 to 94 years; and 3 aged ≥ 95 years.
* **Mean baseline MMSE:** 16.51 (SD 6.737), representing middle-stage dementia.

# YYYInterventions

* **Experimental group:** Active live group music programme, 30 minutes per session, and listening to prerecorded instrumental music, 10 minutes per session, led by 2 musicians.
* **Control group:** Reading group chosen as the control activity to provide a comparable activity. The facilitator of the 40-minute sessions was a trained research assistant.
* Both the active group music programme and control activities ran 3 mornings a week—Monday, Wednesday and Friday—for 8 weeks.
* Facilitators were trained in delivery of the sessions and in working with older people with dementia.

# YYYOutcomes

## Primary outcome

* Agitation measured with the CMAI-SF. Overall and subscale scores were reported for a modified 14-item short form. Timeframe: previous 2 weeks.

## Secondary outcomes

* Anxiety measured with the RAID. Timeframe: previous 2 weeks.
* Quality of life measured with DQOL using overall and subscale score.
* Depression measured with GDS.
* Outcomes measured at baseline, midpoint after the first 8-week intervention arm, and postintervention after the second 8-week intervention arm.

# YYYRisk of Bias

Hardinge approach

Moore approach

* anisometropia of objective spherical equivalent ≤ 1.50 D

* children with ocular or systemic diseases that potentially have an effect on myopia or refractive power

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

2 × 2 factorial, randomised, non-treatment controlled trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** families who attended the antenatal clinic were recruited into the study. Following delivery, the babies were recruited if they were born at term and written informed consent was available from parent(s)/guardian. A family history of atopy was not required for inclusion.

**Exclusion criteria:** infants born pre-term, experience complications due to severe underlying disease were excluded from the study. HBV or HIV positivity of mother at the time of birth or any other inappropriate status as judged by the physician.

# YYYInterventions

* **Synbiotic and skincare (n = 137):** combination of 0.5 g (7 × 10⁹ CFU/g) of *Bifidobacterium bifidum* OLB6378 (Meiji Holdings Co. Ltd., Japan) combined with 0.5 g of fructo-oligosaccharides (Meiji Food Materia Co., Ltd., Japan) twice a day and Locobase® REPAIR Cream (Daiichi Sankyo, Japan), which contains ceramide, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, 2–3 times a day. Intervention was carried out from birth to 6 months of age.
* **Synbiotic only (n = 137):** combination of 0.5 g (7 × 10⁹ CFU/g) of *Bifidobacterium bifidum* OLB6378 (Meiji Holdings Co. Ltd., Japan) combined with 0.5 g of fructo-oligosaccharides (Meiji Food Materia Co., Ltd., Japan) 2× a day from birth to 6 months of age.
* **Skincare only (n = 138):** Locobase® REPAIR Cream (Daiichi Sankyo, Japan), which contains ceramide, cholesterol, and free fatty acids, 2–3 times a day from birth to 6 months.
* **Control (n = 137):** the control group did not receive any synbiotics. The no-treatment group was not prevented from applying emollients due to ethical reasons.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcome:** development of atopic dermatitis by 1 year of age.
* **Secondary outcome:** prevalence of food allergy. Sensitisation to food or inhalant allergens or both. EASI score examined by a paediatrician.
* **Definitions:** atopic dermatitis was diagnosed according to the criteria of the Japanese Dermatological Association (Katayama 2017), and using the UK Working Party’s Diagnostic Criteria (William 1994), included in the questionnaire at 1 year. Defined as itchy rash lasting 2 or more months was reported in the questionnaires returned at 1, 6, and 9 months and 1 year of the baby’s age.
* Food allergy reported in the questionnaire at 1 year. Sensitisation to food or inhalant allergens in total, or both, and allergen-specific IgE levels in blood sampled at 9 months of age.

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Low risk           | A computer-generated randomisation sequence was used for the 2 × 2 factorial allocation. There was no indication that the allocation sequence was compromised.                                                                    |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Some concerns      | The study used a no-treatment control group. Participants and carers were therefore aware of whether synbiotic treatment was received, and the no-treatment group was not prevented from applying emollients for ethical reasons. |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Low risk           | Outcome data were available for a sufficient proportion of participants, and missingness was not considered likely to depend on the true eczema outcome.                                                                          |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Atopic dermatitis was assessed according to the Japanese Dermatological Association and UK Working Party diagnostic criteria, with EASI examination by a paediatrician.                                                           |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The assessment reflected concerns about deviations from intended interventions and selection of the reported result.                                                                                                              |

The review notes that Dissanayake 2018 used no treatment as its comparator and identifies it among studies for which no prespecified analysis plan was available. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Rehabilitation group (n = 30)

"Rehabilitation group received unobstruction exercises after receiving first evaluation. Unobstruction techniques: (a) position of limbs, (b) active and passive exercises of joint of upper and lower limbs including flexion, extension, internal rotation, abduction; actions in each direction repeated 10 to 20 times, (c) bridge movement on bed: patient lay on their back, flexed knee and hip, clamped a small pillow between knees, played breech elevation and hip extension and repeated these actions, (d) wiping or striking suffered limbs up to down with brush or little hammer in order to promote recovery of sensory, (e) transferring and balance exercises

Exercise of sitting balance ability: patient's healthy hand was bound on the tail of bed by a special belt. Head of bed was elevated to 30 degrees. Nurse put patient’s upper limb on trunk, pushed healthy upper limb. This method could enhance strength of extensor muscle of upper limbs and trunk muscle. We increased sitting angle everyday, elongated sitting time and control sitting balance. Exercises from sitting to standing position: nurse stood in front of patient, patient embrace nurse’s waist with healthy hand. Nurse fixed patient’s affected hand on waist. The other hand was put in the subaxillary position of the affected side, which delivered sufficient weight loading to affected side. When patients stood up, nurse called patient's attention to look forward to the direction of nurse’s face. Exercise of standing balance: patients received bedside bridge movement and exercise of lower limb swing in order to practice standing balance ability. Exercise of plain walking: patients walked with supporter or step at first, then feet moved by turn. Nurse also could bind suffered foot and help elevation if needed. Before walking, the lower part of affected limb was hanged in front of chest in order to keep functional position of upper limb and shoulder joint. We should try Chu 2003 to avoid tiredness and try to ensure exercise quality. Exercise of going upstairs and downstairs: according to the rule of 'healthy leg up first, affected leg down first,' training flexor and extensor muscles and joints of lower limbs. Exercise of functions of upper limb and hand: Bobath shaking hands, suffered side upper limb takes assisted active movement with help of healthy side upper limb; inducing upper limb muscle movement and hand performance exercise; patients took flexion and extension of shoulder, elbow, twist and finger joint, grasp, hold and pinch movement. Exercises were performed from easy to difficult, from tough to delicate"

Length of intervention period: varied from "20 days to 14 months with a mean rehabilitation time of 41.3 days"

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "above exercises were taken 1 per day, 40 to 60 min/time"

Intervention provider: nurses

"Two group received routine neurologic treatment and nursing. Control group didn't receive rehabilitation exercise" The individual components delivered are listed in Table 28. Based on the individual components, this intervention is categorised as no intervention.

characteristics_interventions.S:
Caesarean myomectomy vs caesarean section alone.

* **Intervention:** Caesarean myomectomy. The assistant squeezes the myoma towards the endometrium or serosa, then a linear incision at the most prominent part of the myoma was made by electro scalpel till fibroid surface via the myoma pseudocapsule. Surgeon then extracts the fibroid by progressive tractions, while sutuer-ligating the vessels at the basal part to provide hemosta, finally closing tumor cavity using continuous suture method with absorbable 1 Polysorb CL-905, suturing the serosal or endometrium with 2–0 Vicryl. Observe the amount of uterine bleeding after loosening the tourniquet. If the uterine incision is not sutured, the preferred method is to tamp down the uterine cavity with a balloon and, if necessary, ligate the ascending branches of the uterine artery; If the uterine incision has been sutured, it is best to ligate one or both ascending branches of the uterine artery. If necessary, a balloon is inflated into the uterine cavity through the vagina.
* **Control:** Caesarean section

* **Educator:** trained asthma educators
* **Audience:** parent and child

## Intervention groups

There were 2 intervention groups of different intensity. Both arms included in the review.

1. ABC
2. Adherence Monitoring with Feedback Group (AMF)

* **Number:** ABC: 84, 92% completed 6-month and 96% completed 18-month surveys; AMF: 83, 87% completed 6-month and 80% completed 18-month surveys
* **Number, duration and frequency of education sessions:** 5 × 30- to 45-minute home sessions at weeks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 weeks after randomisation

### ABC

Five core components:

1. review of prescribed asthma regimen and training in medication, spacer and peak flow technique;
2. development of an AAP;
3. identification of barriers to accessing health care and problem-solving to remove them;
4. discussion of beliefs and concerns about asthma and medications;
5. provision of written asthma education materials.

### AMF

Received the ABC programme as described above plus the following:

1. objective feedback of medication adherence from an electronic adherence monitor and the asthma educator was trained to provide support in a non-threatening way;
2. families were encouraged to set asthma control goals (e.g. no coughing at night);
3. the importance of positive reinforcement such as verbal praise and low-cost rewards was emphasised. The educator worked with families to identify barriers when goals were not achieved;
4. families were taught strategies to monitor adherence and asthma symptoms by using behavioural charts and symptom diaries, the educator highlighted relationships between improvements in symptoms and adherence where possible.

* **Educational materials used/provided:** written asthma education materials and AAP
* **Incentives:** none but parents were encouraged to provide low-cost rewards and verbal praise as incentives for adherence
* **Compliance:** overall 67% completed all 5 visits, with ABC group 71% and AMF group 63%. Completed 4.0 and 3.8 visits on average for the ABC and AMF intervention groups, respectively.

## Control group

* **Usual care**
* **Number (completed):** 83, 92% completed 6-month and 93% completed 18-month surveys
* **Lost to follow-up:** control group: 84% completed all follow-up; ABC group: 81% completed all follow-up; AMF group: 80% completed all follow-up
* **Withdrawals:** 1 person deceased in AMF group, 1 person deceased in control group

* **Eligibility criteria:** children aged 3–17 years who lived in King County with provider-diagnosed asthma that was either not well controlled or poorly controlled, were enroled in 1 of 2 Medicaid plans, and had a caretaker conversant in either English or Spanish.

# YYYInterventions

* **Educator:** CHW
* **Audience:** caregiver and child
* **Where delivered:** home, also allowing up to 2 telephone contacts in lieu of home visits

## Intervention group

* **Number (completed):** 182 (154)
* **Number, duration and frequency of education sessions:** 4 home visits (allowing for up to 2 telephone contacts in lieu of home visits). Initial visit, then visits at 0.5, 1.5 and 3.5 months later. Also provided as-needed support via telephone, email or additional home visits. Length of session not disclosed.
* **Educational/self-management strategy:** CHW provided education, support and service co-ordination for each household in the intervention. Initial visit to assess the participant’s knowledge of asthma, asthma control level, challenges with controlling asthma, self-management practices and exposure to asthma triggers. Short home visits using motivational interviewing methods. CHWs included children in home visit activities and included them in asthma education, offered coaching on correct use of asthma devices.
* **Programme topics:** “CHWs followed protocols that specified educational content”
* **Incentives:** participants received a USD 10 incentive for completing baseline data collection and USD 35 for completing exit data collection
* **Compliance:** % completed full education programme: 6.6%; partial completion: 91.7%; completed no sessions: 1.6%

## Control group

Usual care. Received asthma education and control resources AFTER exit interview.

* **Number (completed):** 191 (179)
* **Other:** “Participants received a low-emission vacuum cleaner, cleaning supplies, roach abatement supplies (if roaches present) and allergen-impermeable bedding covers” – “both study arms received USD210 worth of asthma control supplies”
* **Lost to follow-up:** intervention group 16; control group 8
* **Withdrawals:** intervention group 12; control group 4

# YYYOutcomes

* **Outcomes measured:** asthma symptom-free days (self-reported number of 24-hour periods during the prior 2 weeks without wheeze, tightness in chest, cough or shortness of breath, a decrease in usual activities because of asthma, or night-time awakening because of asthma), Caregiver QoL (PACQLQ), and asthma-related urgent health services use during the last 12 months (ED, hospitalisation or unscheduled clinic visits – self-reported). Secondary outcomes: asthma episode over 3 months (defined as a time when asthma symptoms were worse, limiting activity more than usual or making you seek medical care for your child), rescue medication use (days per 2 weeks), nights with symptoms (nights per 2 weeks), and asthma control levels (as defined by NAEPP as well controlled, not well controlled, very poorly controlled)
* **Outcomes reported:** as stated
* **Time points:** baseline, then “approximately 1 year after baseline”

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                                                 | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)**                             | Low risk           | Randomisation process clear. “we randomly assigned participants to groups using a permuted block design with varying block size. We stratified randomisation into 4 groups based on age (3–11 years and 12–17 years) and asthma-control level (not well controlled or very poorly controlled), respectively.”                                                                          |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)**                                 | Low risk           | Allocation concealment process described. “sequence numbers and group allocation were concealed in sealed, opaque, numbered envelopes that were centrally prepared and sequentially provided to the CHWs who assigned participants to study groups.”                                                                                                                                   |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias): all outcomes** | Unclear risk       | Although blinding was not possible due to the nature of the intervention, we could not be sure if participants were aware of which intervention they were getting and that educators were aware of which intervention they were delivering.                                                                                                                                            |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias): all outcomes**           | High risk          | Self-reported outcomes in unblinded participants. “A CHW other than the one who provided the intervention collected exit data 1 year later upon study completion.” Unclear who collected data for those in the control group, and if outcome assessors were blinded to reviewing results.                                                                                              |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias): all outcomes**                  | Low risk           | Whilst attrition rate higher in intervention group, used ITT for analyses with a complete case and multiple imputation analysis for each outcome. Intervention group: lost to follow-up: 16; discontinued participation: 12; analysed: 154 in the complete-case analysis, 182 in the multiple imputation analysis. Control group: lost to follow-up: 8, discontinued participation: 4. |
| **Selective reporting (reporting bias)**                                    | Unclear risk       | No predefined protocol available; therefore, unclear if all outcomes intended to be measured were reported on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Other bias**                                                              | High risk          | All outcomes self-reported – outcomes such as ED visits and hospitalisations could have been verified through hospital records, high risk for recall bias.                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

# YYYMethods

* Study design: parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: multi-centre (7 university hospitals in Japan)

* Number randomised: 171 children

* Study follow-up: 2 years

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: 13 (8%) were withdrawn or lost to follow-up

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 9.0 years (range 6-12 years)

* Gender: 74 boys, 94 girls

* Culture: Japanese

* Inclusion criteria:

* aged 6-12 years
* cycloplegic SER between −1.00 D and −6.00 D in both eyes
* anisometropia of objective spherical equivalent ≤ 1.50 D
* astigmatism of ≤ 1.50 D (5) corrected VA ≥ 1.0
* children with normal IOP
* Exclusion criteria:

* abnormal binocular function; amblyopia or manifest strabismus
* children with ocular diseases other than myopia
* children with ocular or systemic diseases that potentially have an effect on myopia or refractive power
* previous or current use of contact lenses, BFs, progressive lenses, or other forms of treatment (including atropine) for myopia
* children with a history of cardiac or respiratory disease
* children with a history of pharmacotherapy for asthma over the past year

# YYYInterventions

* Atropine 0.01% eyedrops (n = 85)

* Placebo eyedrops (n = 86)

# YYYOutcomes

* Primary outcomes

* Change in SER error from baseline (cycloplegic autorefraction)
* Change in AL from baseline (Zeiss IOL Master)
* Secondary outcomes

* Incidence of AEs
* Measurements taken every 6 months for 24 months

* Unit of analysis: data from both eyes included (correlation between eyes adjusted in statistical model)

### ABC

Five core components:

1. review of prescribed asthma regimen and training in medication, spacer and peak flow technique;
2. development of an AAP;
3. identification of barriers to accessing health care and problem-solving to remove them;
4. discussion of beliefs and concerns about asthma and medications;
5. provision of written asthma education materials.

Received the ABC programme as described above plus the following:

Lower extremity rehabilitation training mainly includes muscle strength and coordination function training of affected limbs. The details are as follows.
