characteristics_interventions.S:
* **Educator:** trained Nurse/Health educator. Co-visits with nurses by senior nurse investigators
* **Audience:** child and caregiver of child with asthma
* **Where delivered:** 2 sessions at home, 1 at the general practitioner clinic with the nurse present

## Intervention group

Education plus review at PCP.

* **Number (completed):** 152 (138)
* **Number, duration and frequency of education sessions:** 3 sessions, length not described
* **Educational/self-management strategy:** “For children in the intervention group, the caregiver received asthma education during two home visits including the same topics as the control group. Additionally, during the home visits, the intervention nurse reviewed the caregiver feedback letter that explained the number of the child’s asthma medication fills over the past 12 months, the child’s cotinine concentration, and tips for implementing a total home smoking ban. For the third intervention nurse visit, the nurse joined the caregiver and child at the PCP office for a preventive asthma care visit. During the PCP visit, the nurse delivered a separate clinician feedback letter to the PCP explaining the child’s report of symptom days, inhaler technique, asthma medication fills and cotinine concentration. In addition, the nurse prompted the PCP to deliver a controller medication prescription, address second hand smoke (SHS) exposure for children with any exposure and sign a prepared asthma action plan (AAP) form. The PCP feedback letter included (1) a summary of the child’s symptom frequency, inhaler technique, asthma control and pharmacy; fill report, (2) the child’s cotinine level and (3) recommendations for preventive care based on national asthma guidelines. All feedback letters were developed and signed by a paediatric allergist and a primary care paediatrician. After each PCP visit, the nurse completed an intervention clinic checklist recording (1) PCP review of feedback letter, (2) nurse discussion of controller and rescue medication fills, (3) nurse and parent discussion of cotinine level with PCP and home smoking ban counselling and (4) PCP review of the prepared AAP.”
* **Programme topics:** education about asthma self-management targeting the use of preventer asthma medication, awareness of the child’s exposures to asthma triggers, and importance of asthma preventive care visits. Also device training for PFM and inhaler and spacer, completion of the written AAP. Self-management was defined as “appropriate controller medication use or inhaler device technique in the context of the child’s own environment and particularly for older children.” Specific tips based on the monitoring were given: “You may want to consider a step-up in inhaled steroid medication based on the frequency of daytime wheeze.”
* **Incentives:** caregivers received USD 30 payment for completion of the baseline survey
* **Compliance:** 107 (71%) received all 3 nurse visits. 44 (29%) did not complete the scheduled PCP visits component of the intervention. Reasons for non-completion of the PCP visits included caregiver stressful life events such as hospitalisation or death of a family member, difficulty scheduling PCP visits due to conflicts with caregiver work schedule, child school priorities and lack of belief in preventive care by caregiver.

## Control group

“Children and caregivers assigned to the attention control group received asthma education only during three home visits, including the identification of asthma triggers, medication device training, environmental control education and the importance of controller medication use and preventive asthma care. Caregivers of children assigned to the control received their child’s level of exposure to SHS (cotinine concentration) and tips for implementing a total home smoking ban, by mail at the end of the study.”

* **Number (completed):** 148 (136)
* **Partial completion:** 29%
* **Lost to follow-up:** intervention group 13; control group 12
* **Withdrawals:** intervention group 1 (caregiver death)

The PCP feedback letter included (1) a summary of the child’s symptom frequency, inhaler technique, asthma control and pharmacy; fill report, (2) the child’s cotinine level and (3) recommendations for preventive care based on national asthma guidelines. All feedback letters were developed and signed by a paediatric allergist and a primary care paediatrician. After each PCP visit, the nurse completed an intervention clinic checklist recording (1) PCP review of feedback letter, (2) nurse discussion of controller and rescue medication fills, (3) nurse and parent discussion of cotinine level with PCP and home smoking ban counselling and (4) PCP review of the prepared AAP.”
* **Programme topics:** education about asthma self-management targeting the use of preventer asthma medication, awareness of the child’s exposures to asthma triggers, and importance of asthma preventive care visits. Also device training for PFM and inhaler and spacer, completion of the written AAP. Self-management was defined as “appropriate controller medication use or inhaler device technique in the context of the child’s own environment and particularly for older children.” Specific tips based on the monitoring were given: “You may want to consider a step-up in inhaled steroid medication based on the frequency of daytime wheeze.”
* **Incentives:** caregivers received USD 30 payment for completion of the baseline survey
* **Compliance:** 107 (71%) received all 3 nurse visits. 44 (29%) did not complete the scheduled PCP visits component of the intervention. Reasons for non-completion of the PCP visits included caregiver stressful life events such as hospitalisation or death of a family member, difficulty scheduling PCP visits due to conflicts with caregiver work schedule, child school priorities and lack of belief in preventive care by caregiver.

## Control group

“Children and caregivers assigned to the attention control group received asthma education only during three home visits, including the identification of asthma triggers, medication device training, environmental control education and the importance of controller medication use and preventive asthma care. Caregivers of children assigned to the control received their child’s level of exposure to SHS (cotinine concentration) and tips for implementing a total home smoking ban, by mail at the end of the study.”

* **Number (completed):** 148 (136)
* **Partial completion:** 29%
* **Lost to follow-up:** intervention group 13; control group 12
* **Withdrawals:** intervention group 1 (caregiver death)

# YYYOutcomes

* **Outcomes measured:** primary outcome: the number of preventive asthma care visits with a PCP (number of visits over past 6 months at every 6 months data point as reported by caregiver). Secondary outcome: number of ED visits over 12 months (number of visits over past 6 months at every 6 months data point as reported by caregiver). Additional health outcomes measured: asthma severity (based on daytime and night-time symptom frequency over past 2 weeks) and control (NAEPP definitions: well controlled, not well controlled or very poorly controlled based on the number of symptom days and nights, rescue medication use, activity limitation and number of ED visits and hospitalisations). Also looked at asthma medication use (pharmacy dispensation records) and SHS exposure (child saliva samples collected for cotinine analysis using enzyme immunoassay analysis (cotinine cut off level of 1.0 ng/mL used to define positive SHS exposure)). Looked also at asthma management stress (self-reported by caregivers using visual analogue scale, with 0 = no stress and 10 = highest possible level of asthma caregiving stress), life stress (Perceived Stress Scale: 4 item, total score 0–16, higher scores reflective of more perceived stress), social support (emotional/informational support subscale of the Medical Outcomes Study: 8 items, higher scores indicating greater perceived social support) and caregiver QoL (caregivers completed the Activity Limitations Scale of the PACQLQ as a measure of QoL).
* **Outcomes reported:** symptom-free days in past 14 days, change in symptom-free days, symptom-free nights past 14 days, asthma control, total ED visits, total hospitalisations, number of PCP visits, cotinine exposure, medication (preventer) use, pharmacy fills at 12 months
* **Time points:** baseline, reported 12-month follow-up.

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                                                 | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)**                             | Low risk           | Randomisation process clear. “children were randomly assigned using random-number generation and stratified by child age (3–5 versus 6–10 years).”                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)**                                 | Low risk           | Allocation concealment process described. “the Project Coordinator assigned children to the intervention or control groups using a series of numbered opaque envelopes that had been pre-randomised in blocks of two by child’s age.”                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias): all outcomes** | Unclear risk       | Although blinding was not possible due to the nature of the intervention, we could not be sure if participants were aware of which intervention they were getting and that educators were aware of which intervention they were delivering.                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias): all outcomes**           | High risk          | Self-reported outcomes in unblinded participants.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias): all outcomes**                  | Low risk           | Balanced numbers of attrition between intervention and control group.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Selective reporting (reporting bias)**                                    | High risk          | Secondary outcomes in the NCT record differed from those reported in the primary publication (primary outcome measures reported in NCT record: number of primary care appointments kept over 12 months; secondary outcome measures reported in NCT record: number of refills for anti-inflammatory medications prescribed over 12 months) – reported on more outcomes than originally stated in protocol. |
| **Other bias**                                                              | High risk          | Outcomes were all caregiver self-reported; however, could have been verified, therefore at high risk for recall bias.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

characteristics_interventions.S:
Caesarean myomectomy vs caesarean section alone.

* **Intervention:** Caesarean myomectomy. There were 2 intervention arms:

  1. Endometrial Myomectomy
  2. Serosal Myomectomy

For the endometrial myomectomy, following the delivery of the newborn and placenta, the incision at the lower uterine segment was assessed. Then the bleeding foci were clamped, a sterile gauze was put on the lower uterine incision and fibroids were inspected beneath endometrium by mild inversion of the uterine walls. In case the visualization of fibroids was difficult due to the uterine contractions, bivalves were used to support the dissection plane. After an endometrial incision was made, fibroids were removed by blunt and sharp dissection and myoma pseudocapsules were spared. Any vascular structures at the bottom of the fibroids were clamped and sutured. The incision sites were repaired with a separate or figure of eight sutures using absorbable material. Following the maintenance of hemostasis and uterine tonus, the incision at the lower uterine segment was restored.

For the serosal myomectomy, all procedures until the closure of lower uterine segment are the same as EM. The serosal surface of the uterus was topographically evaluated for the presence and type of the leiomyomas. Leiomyomas close to each other were removed from a single incision in order to diminish the adhesion formation. A linear incision over uterine serosa by electro scalpel till fibroid surface via the myoma pseudocapsule, then an exposition of the cleavage plan between fibroid and myoma pseudocapsule. Surgeon then extracts the fibroid by progressive tractions, while selectively coagulating the superficial vessels of the pseudocapsule to provide hemostasis, finally closing hysterotomy by continuous introflexing sutures (basketball sutures) and, eventually, intravenous oxytocin administration.

* **Control:** Caesarean section

characteristics_risk_of_bias.S:
| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Randomisation process** | Low risk of bias | Randomisation was performed using a lens allocation table designed on Microsoft Excel. Allocation concealment was maintained until after enrollment and participants assigned. There were no baseline imbalances that would suggest a problem with randomisation. |
| **Deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk of bias | Participants, carers and those delivering the intervention were unaware of intervention received. Results analysed using ITT principles |
| **Missing outcome data** | High risk of bias | Outcome data were not available for all, or nearly all, randomized participants, and there is no evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data, and no information on whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value. |
| **Measurement of the outcome** | Low risk of bias | Appropriate and comparable methods of measuring outcome data were used. Outcome assessors may have been aware of the group allocation, but bias is minimised by using objective measurements. Therefore, it is unlikely that the outcome was influenced by knowledge of the intervention received. |
| **Selection of the reported results** | Some concerns | Protocol registered. Not enough information in the protocol on a statistical plan and no published statistical plan found. |
| **Overall** | High risk of bias | The study is judged to be at high risk of bias in at least one domain for this result. |

# YYYMethods

* Study design: parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: multi-centre (Okayama University Medical School, Japan; Eye Hospital of Wenzhou Medical College, China; Eulji University, South Korea)

* Number randomised: 197 children (120 from China and 77 from Japan)

* Study follow-up: 2 years

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: the trial in South Korea was terminated after 12 months due to protocol violation and the data were not included; 28/197 (14%) did not complete 2 years of follow-up

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 10 years (range 6-12 years)

* Gender: 95 boys, 74 girls

* Culture: Chinese and Japanese children

* Inclusion criteria:

* age 6-12 years
* SER error between −0.50 D and −4.50 D
* astigmatism ≤ 1.50 D
* anisometropia ≤ 1.50 in spherical or cylindrical error
* BCVA of 6/9 (20/30) or better in each eye
* normal ocular and general health
* willingness to wear spectacle lenses continuously
* willingness and ability to tolerate cycloplegia
* informed parental consent
* Exclusion criteria:

* amblyopia or manifested squint
* history of rigid contact lens or BF contact lens wear
* use of BF or progressive lenses or other myopia treatment in previous 12 months
* abnormal binocular function
* vestibular disorders or motor imbalance
* any systemic condition affecting refractive development or vision, or any condition precluding adherence to the study protocol (e.g. not available for follow-up for 2 years)

# YYYInterventions

* PA-PALs +1.0 D (n = 67): positively aspherised PALs with +1.00 D add

* PA-PALs +1.5 D (n = 63): positively aspherised PALs with +1.50 D add

* SVLs (n = 67)

* Note: all lenses are worn during normal waking hours

# YYYOutcomes

* Primary outcomes

* Refractive error, measured by cycloplegic autorefraction
* AL, measured by IOL Master (Carl Zeiss Meditec)
* Secondary outcome: peripheral refractive error, measured using an open field autorefractor

* Measurements taken at baseline and at 6, 12, 18, and 24 months

* Unit of analysis: eye (both eyes of each child analysed)

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Randomisation process** | Low risk of bias | Randomisation was performed using a lens allocation table designed on Microsoft Excel. Allocation concealment was maintained until after enrollment and participants assigned. There were no baseline imbalances that would suggest a problem with randomisation. |
| **Deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk of bias | Participants, carers and those delivering the intervention were unaware of intervention received. Results analysed using ITT principles |
| **Missing outcome data** | High risk of bias | Outcome data were not available for all, or nearly all, randomized participants, and there is no evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data, and no information on whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value. |
| **Measurement of the outcome** | Low risk of bias | Appropriate and comparable methods of measuring outcome data were used. Outcome assessors may have been aware of the group allocation, but bias is minimised by using objective measurements. Therefore, it is unlikely that the outcome was influenced by knowledge of the intervention received. |
| **Selection of the reported results** | Some concerns | Protocol registered. Not enough information in the protocol on a statistical plan and no published statistical plan found. |
| **Overall** | High risk of bias | The study is judged to be at high risk of bias in at least one domain for this result. |

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

* Study design: parallel-group RCT, with run-in period

* Study centre: single (the Ohio State University College of Optometry, USA)

* Number randomised: 116 children

* Study follow-up: 3 years

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: none

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 10.7 years (range 8-12 years)

* Gender: 47 boys, 69 girls

* Culture: Columbus, Ohio, USA; 84.5% white (not of Hispanic origin), 8.6% Asian or Pacific Islander, 4.3% black (not of Hispanic origin)

* Inclusion criteria:

* 8-11 years old at time of randomisation
* myopia with SER error between −0.75 D and −4.00 D in each eye, as measured by cycloplegic refraction
* corrected VA of 20/20 or better in each eye
* Exclusion criteria:

* astigmatism > 1.50 DC in each eye by cycloplegic refraction or > 1.00 DC on manifest refraction
* previous or attempted history of contact lens wear
* anisometropia > 1.00 D between eyes
* eye disease and binocular vision problems
* systemic disease that may affect vision or vision development
* Note: all participants had to successfully complete a run-in period before enrolment into the study to exclude those who could not adapt to rigid contact lenses; 32 children did not complete the run-in period and were excluded. Success for the run-in period was defined as wearing the lenses at least 40 h/week and stating that the lenses were "always comfortable" or "usually comfortable"

# YYYInterventions

* (n = 59): RGPs worn during waking hours for 3 years

* (n = 57): soft contact lenses worn during waking hours for 3 years

* Note: prescription changes were made by an unmasked examiner based on participant complaints and improvement in VA

# YYYOutcomes

* Primary outcome

* Change in cycloplegic autorefraction during 3 years (spherical equivalent)
* Secondary outcomes

* Change in AL
* Change in peripheral autorefraction
* Change in crystalline lens curvatures
* Change in corneal curvature and thickness
* Change in accommodation
* Change in IOP
* Measurements taken at baseline and every 6 months for 3 years

* Unit of analysis: data analysed for right eye only

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Randomisation process** | Some concerns | Randomisation was performed using stratification and block allocation. There was no information relating to allocation concealment. There were no baseline imbalances that would suggest a problem with randomisation. |
| **Deviations from intended interventions** | Some concerns | It was not possible to mask the participants due to functional differences in interventions being studied. Investigator providing clinical care and obtaining measurements were masked to group allocation. No information on deviation from intended outcomes. Data were analysed using ITT methods. |
| **Missing outcome data** | Low risk of bias | Data available for approx 97% of participants. |
| **Measurement of the outcome** | Low risk of bias | Appropriate methods of measuring outcome data were used. Same study protocol for all participants and the team were masked to the group allocation of patients. |
| **Selection of the reported results** | Some concerns | The outcome measurements were taken in accordance with the clinical trials registry record. No statistical analysis plan (SAP) was reported. |
| **Overall** | Some concerns | The study is judged to raise some concerns in at least one domain for this result, but not to be at high risk of bias for any domain. |

# YYYMethods

Prospective randomised controlled single-centre clinical trial.

Exclusions after randomisation: none reported.

Losses to follow-up: none reported.

Period: December 2008 to December 2012.

Duration of follow-up: 12–42 months (mean 24 months).

# YYYParticipants

Country: China.

Participants: 66 (stenting plus CDT (test group): 27; CDT (control): 39).

Age: mean 50.85 ± 1.95 years (range 18–70 years).

Sex: male 26 (39%) and female 40 (61%).

Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 70 years; new-onset DVT; the course of disease no longer than 15 days; complete patency of the major branch of the distal iliac vein after CDT with residual stenosis of > 50%; signed informed consent; no contraindications for thrombolytic and anticoagulant therapy.

Exclusion criteria: Patients with severe renal impairment (Cr CL < 30 mL/min); patients in a terminal stage of cancer with a life expectancy of < 3 months, pregnancy, patients with congenital coagulation defects and patients reporting previous or current use of thrombolytic procedures, including surgery and thrombolysis.

# YYYInterventions

Angioplasty or stenting: In the test group, balloon dilatation and stent (diameter: 12–14 mm, length: 6–12 cm) were performed through the lesser saphenous vein, the great saphenous vein, the pretibial vein, or the popliteal vein; residual stenosis < 10% was acceptable.

Control: “The patients in the control group were given the same treatment after the thrombolytic catheters were removed.” No stent was implanted in the control group.

Co-treatment: All participants underwent implantation of an inferior vena cava filter. A 4F Uni*fuse catheter was inserted until the deep vein of affected extremity, including femoro-popliteal segments, through the lesser saphenous vein (n = 46; 69.70%), the great saphenous vein (n = 10; 15.15%), the pretibial vein (n = 5; 7.58%), or the popliteal vein (n = 5; 7.58%); residual stenosis < 10% was acceptable. No participants received intervention by femoral vein access. No further details about puncture, such as ultrasound aid, were given. Urokinase 4400 units/kg/h for 24h; dosage was adjusted according to patient age, bleeding tendency, and rate of blood coagulation. Following thrombolysis, intermittent deep vein venography was performed to determine residual stenosis. If it was > 50%, participants were randomised. Average duration of postoperative urokinase infusion was 4.24 ± 0.30 days (range 2–15 days) in all participants. LMWH was simultaneously injected subcutaneously twice daily (4000–5000 units every 12 hours) for a minimum of 7 days during CDT. Then, warfarin was given orally for anticoagulation until INR 2–3 for at least 6 months. After discharge from the hospital, participants were advised to wear compression stockings and use oral drugs to promote blood flow (e.g. aescine sodium or diosmin).

  * Number who have had previous ear surgery: not reported
  * Number who had previous antibiotic treatment for CSOM: not reported

* History of purulent otorrhoea lasting > 1 year
* People who were examined carefully and diagnosed with CSOM

* History of general health problems
* Did not use the topical solutions regularly

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.

# YYYParticipants

**Inclusion criteria:** pregnant, atopic women. Maternal atopy defined as doctor-diagnosed clinical history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eczema plus a positive SPT to 1 or more common allergens.

**Exclusion criteria:** women excluded if smoked, had other medical problems or pregnancy complications, delivered before 37 weeks’ gestation, or already taking probiotic supplements.

# YYYInterventions

* **Treatment (n = 115):** 3 × 10⁹/L *L. acidophilus* LAVRI-A1 in maltodextrin (Probiomics, Sydney, Australia). Supplements supplied as stable freeze-dried powder, dissolved in 1 to 2 mL sterile water and administered orally daily from birth to 6 months.
* **Control (n = 111):** maltodextrin alone.
* Intervention commenced within 48 hours of delivery and was given only to the baby, independent of feeding method.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcomes:** clinical assessment of atopic dermatitis at 6 and 12 months of age. Incidence of atopic dermatitis, food allergy, and sensitisation at 12 months and 2.5 years of age. Primary allergy prevention in a population of Australian children at high risk of allergic disease.
* **Other outcomes:** detailed history and examination collected at 12 months and 2.5 years by the same paediatric allergist. Other symptoms based on parental record; all parents who noted “noisy breathing” of any kind were asked to give detailed descriptions of this to the paediatrician. Doctor-diagnosed gastrointestinal infections were recorded. Assessment of the expression of T-regulatory phenotype.
* **Atopic dermatitis:** typical skin lesions responsive to topical steroids. The severity determined using the severity score of atopic dermatitis (SCORAD).
* **IgE-mediated food allergy:** history of immediate symptoms after contact with or ingestion of food and a positive SPT to the implicated food. Symptoms of acute food allergy include skin reactions (hives, rash or swelling) or respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, stridor) or gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, vomiting, loose stools) or cardiovascular symptoms (collapse).
* **Asthma:** defined as recurrent wheezing (3 or more episodes, at least 1 confirmed by a paediatrician or general practitioner) with evidence of responsiveness to bronchodilator therapy.

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain                                            | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bias arising from the randomisation process**        | Some concerns      | There were significant differences in birth length and birth head circumference between the groups analysed.                                                                                                                                          |
| **Bias due to deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk           | Participants, carers and trial personnel were blinded. Intervention was administered independently of feeding method, and there was no evidence of important deviations caused by the trial context.                                                  |
| **Bias due to missing outcome data**                   | Low risk           | For the infant food-allergy outcome, missing data were not considered sufficient to place the result at serious risk of bias. The review’s concern about substantial loss to follow-up applied to the later five-year childhood-incidence assessment. |
| **Bias in measurement of the outcome**                 | Low risk           | Food allergy required a history of immediate symptoms following food exposure and a positive skin-prick test to the implicated food. Assessment was conducted by the same paediatric allergist.                                                       |
| **Bias in selection of the reported result**           | Some concerns      | A prespecified analysis plan was not available.                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Overall bias**                                       | Some concerns      | The assessment reflected concerns about the randomisation process and selection of the reported result.                                                                                                                                               |

The review directly attributes some concerns in the randomisation domain to significant differences in birth length and head circumference, and identifies Taylor 2006 among studies lacking an available prespecified analysis plan. ([PubMed Central (PMC)][1])

characteristics_interventions.S:
Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. The surgical patients received the best medical treatment as well as surgery. Open craniotomy was performed with microscopic haematoma removal with a suction device. The clot was thoroughly evacuated, leaving only thin layers of coagulum adherent to particularly friable brain tissue. In most cases, satisfactory haemostasis was achieved with the use of cottonoids so that bipolar cauterisation of small blood vessels was rarely necessary. Epidural drains were routinely placed and the patients were returned to the ICU. Median time from symptom onset to surgery 7 hours (IQR 6 - 8).

Standard medical management group : best medical treatment without surgery. Decision on endotracheal intubation made early in emergency department and directed by respiratory failure. Initiation of antihypertensive treatment (reduction of hypertension by 20% from baseline) when SBP ≥180 mm Hg, DBP ≥105 mm Hg, or MAP ≥130 mm Hg; in emergency department with repeated intravenous boluses of short-acting agents, and steady control in the ICU with continuous infusions of antihypertensive agents. Emergency ICP control measures for comatose patients included optimal head positioning, mannitol administration, and hyperventilation to a PCO2 of 28-32 mm Hg. Initiation of invasive ICP monitoring in the ICU for patients with a GCS score ≤8, with a target CPP at 70-100 mm Hg. Initiation of hyperventilation to a pCO2 of 25-30 mmHg if ICP remained >20 mm Hg despite osmotherapy with mannitol. Aggressively lowering of elevated core body temperature using antipyretics with additional cooling blankets and ice when necessary. # YYYMethods

Study design : parallel RCT. Total study duration : one year (participant enrolment). Details of any 'run in' period : not reported. Number of study centres and location : single-centre: Thriassio hospital, Greece. Date of study : January 1998 – December 2003 (participant enrolment).

# YYYParticipants

Number randomised : not explicitly reported, only that “there were 108 patients diagnosed with primary subcortical or putaminal haemorrhage who fulfilled the study entry criteria”. Number lost to follow-up : not reported. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : not reported. Number analysed : 108 (surgical group: 54; conservative group: 54). Number of cross-overs : 1 in the control group (neurological deterioration); none in the surgical group.

Baseline characteristics: mean age 61.4 years (SD 15.5) with range 31 - 80 years, male sex 56%, mean GCS score 8.8 (SD 4.7), mean ICH volume 56 mL (SD 24.5). ICH location: 47% lobar, 53% deep, 0% thalamic involvement (exclusion criterion), 52% left hemispheric. IVH extension not reported. No baseline imbalances between the surgical and standard medical management group.

Inclusion criteria :

* Spontaneous supratentorial ICH diagnosed by CT.

* ICH volume > 30 mL.

* Focal neurological deficit and/or impaired level of consciousness.

* Initiation of surgical or medical treatment <8 hours post-ictus.

Exclusion criteria :

* CT scan suggestive of underlying structural vascular abnormality, such as aneurysm or AVM, or an angiography finding positive for either of these entities.

* Age >80 years.

* Patients with thalamic haemorrhage.

* Patients with a GCS score of 15.

* Terminal medical illness

* Coagulopathy.

* Administration of anticoagulants.

* Trauma.

* Pregnancy.

* Lack of informed consent.

# YYYInterventions

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. The surgical patients received the best medical treatment as well as surgery. Open craniotomy was performed with microscopic haematoma removal with a suction device. The clot was thoroughly evacuated, leaving only thin layers of coagulum adherent to particularly friable brain tissue. In most cases, satisfactory haemostasis was achieved with the use of cottonoids so that bipolar cauterisation of small blood vessels was rarely necessary. Epidural drains were routinely placed and the patients were returned to the ICU. Median time from symptom onset to surgery 7 hours (IQR 6 - 8).

Standard medical management group : best medical treatment without surgery. Decision on endotracheal intubation made early in emergency department and directed by respiratory failure. Initiation of antihypertensive treatment (reduction of hypertension by 20% from baseline) when SBP ≥180 mm Hg, DBP ≥105 mm Hg, or MAP ≥130 mm Hg; in emergency department with repeated intravenous boluses of short-acting agents, and steady control in the ICU with continuous infusions of antihypertensive agents. Emergency ICP control measures for comatose patients included optimal head positioning, mannitol administration, and hyperventilation to a PCO2 of 28-32 mm Hg. Initiation of invasive ICP monitoring in the ICU for patients with a GCS score ≤8, with a target CPP at 70-100 mm Hg. Initiation of hyperventilation to a pCO2 of 25-30 mmHg if ICP remained >20 mm Hg despite osmotherapy with mannitol. Aggressively lowering of elevated core body temperature using antipyretics with additional cooling blankets and ice when necessary. Isotonic fluids were administered as the standard intravenous replacement fluids. Enteral feeding commenced within 48 hours after ictus. Anticonvulsants (phenytoin or valproic acid) were given to reduce the risk of early seizures in patients with subcortical haematomas. In the absence of seizures, the prophylactic antiepileptic treatment was discontinued after 1 month. Therapy also included gastric cytoprotection, maintenance of normoglycemia, early nutritional support, and deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis with low-dose subcutaneous heparin started on day 2 after ictus. Physiotherapy was directed toward maintaining both limb mobility and pulmonary ventilation. Whenever possible, patients were taken out of bed and mobilised at the earliest reasonable time. Occupational therapy, speech therapy, and rehabilitation services were consulted as soon as medically feasible.

Concomitant interventions : none.

# YYYOutcomes

Mortality at 1 year; good functional outcome assessed with the GOS (GOS score >3) at 1 year.

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Random sequence generation (selection bias)** | Unclear risk | Insufficient information is provided to assess whether the allocation sequence generation was adequate, as the used sequence generation is incompletely defined and the use of some random component in the process is not confirmed. Quote: “The study statistician provided a list of random sequential assignment of cases to conservative or surgical treatment." |
| **Allocation concealment (selection bias)** | Unclear risk | Randomisation was conducted using envelopes. However, the minimal criteria for a judgement of adequate concealment of allocation sequence were not met as it is unclear whether the envelopes were also sequentially numbered, opaque and sealed. Quote: “Each patient assignment was placed in a numbered envelope, which was opened after signed informed consent has been obtained." |
| **Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias) All outcomes** | High risk | Participants and local investigators were not blinded to treatment allocation. |
| **Blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) All outcomes** | Unclear risk | Outcome assessments were performed by the physician investigator, who was not involved in the prior treatment of patients. It is unclear whether the physician investigator was blinded for treatment allocation. |
| **Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias) All outcomes** | Unclear risk | Only the number of “patients diagnosed with primary subcortical or putaminal haemorrhage who fulfilled the study entry criteria” is described. The number of participants randomised into each treatment group is not explicitly reported, and therefore, it is unclear whether there is missing outcome data. |
| **Selective reporting (reporting bias)** | High risk | Follow-up evaluation was performed at two months, six months and one year after randomisation, but good functional outcome was only reported at one year. Mortality is only reported for both groups separately at one year (at day four and one month, only the combined results are reported, and mortality at two and six months is not reported). |
| **Other bias** | Low risk | No evidence of other sources of bias. |

characteristics_interventions.S:
Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. Frontotemporal or pterional craniotomy with haematoma evacuation under microscopic guidance. Pharmacological blood pressure reduction by about 25% after induction of anaesthesia, with infusion of mannitol (1.0 g/kg of body weight) during the craniotomy. Thorough evacuation of clot, leaving only thin layers of coagulum adherent to particularly friable brain surfaces. In case of persistently bleeding offending lenticulostriate branches, they were selectively cauterised. After decompression was achieved, the SBP was further decreased to approximately 150 mm Hg, and from that point tightly controlled with a 150 mm Hg ceiling. Routine placement of epidural drains. Postoperative management of the patient’s airway consistent with standard postoperative care, but hyperventilation was not performed. Average time from symptom onset to surgery not reported.

Standard medical management group : a combination of two groups (for the synthesis of this review):

* Best medical management (BMM) : management in a medical ICU with the internal medicine service serving as primary physicians. Dexamethasone therapy (4 mg i.v. every 6 hours), with tapering of dosage over 7 to 14 days. Administration of appropriate antihypertensive drugs, with the goal of decreasing SBP by 25% over the first 24 hours, then slowly decreasing the target blood pressure over the next 48 - 72 hours to high-normal levels. Intermittent diuresis with furosemide and mannitol every 4 - 6 hours empirically over the first several days, with more or less frequent administration depending on the neurologic progress of the patient as well as the systemic tolerance. Intubation and mechanical hyperventilation (target pCO2 of 20 to 25 mm Hg) in all patients with decreased level of consciousness (grades 2 and 3) and in grade 1 patients who were neurologically deteriorating or who showed pulmonary compromise.

* BMM plus ICP monitoring : managed exactly as those in the BMM arm, with the exception of the placement of a frontal ventriculostomy (usually contralateral to haematoma), connected to a pressure monitor and a drainage system. The medical regimens of diuresis and hyperventilation were employed to maintain ICP levels of <20 mm Hg. When medical therapy was unsuccessful at achieving this level of control, intermittent CSF drainage was added to the treatment protocol.

Concomitant interventions : none.

Notes : target sample size was 60. The trial was prematurely stopped as a result of slow patient accrual and poor functional outcome in all treatment groups. The trial has three treatment arms (best medical management, best medical management plus ICP monitoring, and surgical evacuation). For the synthesis of this review, the best medical management and best medical management plus ICP monitoring groups, were combined as the comparator intervention.

# YYYParticipants

The numbers randomised : 21 (surgical group: 8; control group: 13 (9 in the best medical management group and 4 in best medical management plus ICP monitoring group)). Number lost to follow-up : none. Number missing (exclusions & withdrawals) : none. Number analysed : 21 (surgical group: 8; control group: 13). Number of cross-overs : none (cross-over was not permitted).

Baseline characteristics : mean age 54.0 years (SD 9.9). ICH location: 100% deep (inclusion criterion) and 0% lobar. IVH extension 0%. Sex, GCS score and ICH volume are not reported. * CT evidence of classic putaminal haemorrhage ≥3.0 cm in diameter with or without ventricular extension.

* Documented history of hypertension (minimal prior recorded blood pressure of 160/95 mmHg).

Exclusion criteria :

* Aneurysm, AVM, or tumour (angiography required).

* Patients with decorticate or decerebrate posturing.

* Any patient with an unassociated neurologic illness, end-stage systemic disease (e.g. renal, cardiac, hepatic, or neoplastic), or coagulopathy.

Surgical group : craniotomy with haematoma evacuation. Frontotemporal or pterional craniotomy with haematoma evacuation under microscopic guidance. * Best medical management (BMM) : management in a medical ICU with the internal medicine service serving as primary physicians. Intubation and mechanical hyperventilation (target pCO2 of 20 to 25 mm Hg) in all patients with decreased level of consciousness (grades 2 and 3) and in grade 1 patients who were neurologically deteriorating or who showed pulmonary compromise.

Functional outcome assessed with own outcome scale at 3 months and 6 months (outcome Grade 3 and 4 on a 4-item scale was considered “good functional outcome” (= independent at home or returns to prestroke social activity but not necessarily to occupation)).

characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Rehabilitation

"The training contents mainly included:

(1) Physical rehabilitation training: 1) After the patient regains consciousness, according to the actual situation of the patient, according to the principle of training strength from weak to strong, and training time from short to long, the patient is trained, 30min/time, 1~2 times/cL 2) If the patient's condition is more serious, help the patient to turn over (3h/time) and slap the patient's back at the same time; at the same time, properly change the body position (mainly the lateral position and the supine position) to prevent foot drop and foot valgus. In addition, the patient should be given full body massage, and appropriate limb training should be carried out accord- Meng Fanda 2021 ing to the specific conditions of the patients, such as body training, turning over the affected and healthy limbs, etc. (3min/time). Upper limb rehabilitation. 3) Lower extremity training: After the patient's condition is stable, the patient can be guided to perform standing and balance rehabilitation training. By getting up and standing on the bed, gradually move towards independent standing and walking. If necessary, a lower extremity orthosis can be used for auxiliary training. The training process follows a step-by-step principle. 4) After the patient's physical activity has improved, the patient can be guided to perform exercises such as swimming and Tai Chi (3min/time), and the weight-bearing time can be gradually extended to train the strength of the lower limbs.

(2) Language rehabilitation training. Starting from simple pronunciation, according to the order from easy to difficult, the patients are given language rehabilitation training, 30min/time, 1~2 times/d."

(2) Routine care

"The control group received routine nursing care, which mainly included routine medication guidance, dietary guidance, and psychological guidance. "

characteristics_interventions.S:
## General details

* **Surgeon:** Not reported

* **Components:** Cobalt chrome alloy stem, bipolar head, 41 press-fit, 2 cemented stem

* **Anaesthesia:** Not reported

* **Care protocol:** After admission, patients were actively treated for comorbidities, underwent preoperative preparation, and received preoperative education. Once the preoperative preparation was completed, the surgery was scheduled. Both procedures were performed with the patient in a standard lateral position. There were no specific positioning requirements for the SuperPATH group. However, for the anterolateral group, special restrictions were applied: "D-shaped shoe," internal rotation of the lower limbs, and abduction. When lying on the unaffected side, a pillow was placed between the legs to prevent adduction and external rotation of the lower limb. Both groups received prophylactic anticoagulant medication, using rivaroxaban, which continued as part of their ongoing treatment. After the anaesthesia wore off, active movement was encouraged. For the SuperPATH group, patients were encouraged to walk with the assistance of a walking aid or crutches on the second day after surgery, without any specific range of motion restrictions. For the anterolateral group, patients were allowed to walk on the ground after one week, with toes pointing forward. They were instructed to avoid hip flexion exceeding 90°, external rotation of the affected limb, and crossing their legs for six months. Regular follow-up examinations were scheduled at 3 and 6 months postoperatively, and then annually.

## Intervention group 1 (Posterior)

"Conventional Instrumentation SuperPATH Approach (Experimental Group) [5-7]: The hip joint was flexed to approximately 60°, internally rotated by 20°, and slightly adducted. Along the axis of the femur, a longitudinal incision was made starting approximately 2 cm below the tip of the greater trochanter, extending proximally for about 8 cm. The gluteus maximus muscle was bluntly separated and retracted to expose the gluteus medius muscle. Instead of using the specialised retractor for SuperPATH technique, a conventional "S" hook was used to retract the gluteus medius muscle anteriorly, revealing the piriformis muscle and the gluteus minimus muscle. At this point, unnamed vessels crossing the surgical field were often visible, and electrocoagulation was performed to control bleeding and avoid interference with the surgical process. Access was gained through the gap between the piriformis and gluteus minimus muscles, entering the joint capsule beneath. The capsule could be incised in a "T" or "L" shape, revealing the femoral neck and acetabulum, as well as the intertrochanteric fossa and the apex of the greater trochanter. Two commonly used acetabular hooks were used instead of the specialised blunt hook for SuperPATH, inserted along the anterior and posterior aspects of the femoral neck cortex, allowing simultaneous retraction of the joint capsule and surrounding muscle groups, resulting in good exposure of the surgical field. Under direct visualization, fracture reduction could usually be easily achieved, which helped determine the anteversion angle (or based on the residual axis of the fracture ends). A Kirschner wire could be used as a substitute for SuperPATH to determine the direction of the femoral medullary cavity."

## Intervention group 2 (Lateral)

"Conventional Instrumentation Anterolateral Approach (Control Group) [8]: A modified Hardinge approach was used, where the iliotibial tract was bluntly separated, and the gluteus medius muscle was retracted. The anterior one-third of the gluteus medius muscle and the gluteus minimus muscle were cut near their insertions, and the retracted muscles were then mobilized inward. This provided good exposure to the anterior aspect of the joint capsule, which was then excised. The femoral neck was preserved approximately 1.0 cm, and osteotomy was performed to remove the femoral head. The diameter was measured, and an appropriate femoral head was selected. The femoral side was opened, the medullary canal was reamed distally, and the proximal portion was shaped. After successful completion, the joint was irrigated, and the prosthesis was implanted. In the case of a cemented prosthesis, a medullary canal plug was placed, followed by insertion of an exhaust tube. After injecting bone cement, the exhaust tube was removed, and the femoral stem containing the intermediate component was inserted, ensuring no overflow. After solidification, neck length was checked, and the dual articulation head was installed. Finally, reduction was performed, and the joint was tested for movement in all directions without impingement, stable and not dislocating, with good tension. Extensive irrigation was performed, and approximately 50 mL of tranexamic acid solution was injected into the surrounding soft tissues to reduce bleeding. After confirming no active bleeding, the joint capsule was sutured and repaired, and the decision to place a drain was based on the presence of exudate. The incision was closed."

After solidification, neck length was checked, and the dual articulation head was installed. Finally, reduction was performed, and the joint was tested for movement in all directions without impingement, stable and not dislocating, with good tension. Extensive irrigation was performed, and approximately 50 mL of tranexamic acid solution was injected into the surrounding soft tissues to reduce bleeding. After confirming no active bleeding, the joint capsule was sutured and repaired, and the decision to place a drain was based on the presence of exudate. The incision was closed."

# YYYMethods

| **Study design**                  | Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial                                                                                  |

| **Setting**                       | Single center (San Francisco General Hospital, San Francisco, California, USA)                                                      |
| **Power calculation/sample size** | To detect a 4.5-minute difference between groups, two-tailed hypothesis with alpha error 0.05 and 95% power, 78 participants needed |
| **Ethics**                        | Study approved by Committee on Human Research of the University of California, San Francisco                                        |
| **Publication status**            | Published as full study                                                                                                             |

# YYYParticipants

* **Inclusion criteria:** People seeking abortion procedures between 12 weeks 6 days and 15 weeks 6 days verified by ultrasound, English/Spanish speaking, good health, > 18 years old.
* **Exclusion criteria:** More than 1 prior cesarean delivery, multiple gestation, fetal demise, documented cervical or lower uterine segment myoma (> 3 cm), history of prior cone biopsy or loop electrosurgical excision procedure, bleeding disorder or anticoagulation therapy, IUD in place, allergy to misoprostol, breastfeeding and unwilling to temporarily discard milk.
* **Number of participants randomized:** 84 (1 participant in misoprostol group failed to appear on second day for procedure).

# YYYInterventions

* **Group A (n = 42): misoprostol.** Day 1: placebo (speculum exam with sham placement). Day 2 (procedure day): 400 µg misoprostol placed in the posterior fornix of the vagina 3 to 4 hours prior to the procedure.
* **Group B (n = 42): laminaria.** Day 1: overnight laminaria. Day 2 (procedure day): 2 placebo tablets (vitamin B6) placed in the posterior fornix of the vagina 3 to 4 hours prior to the procedure.

# YYYOutcomes

* **Primary outcome:** Procedure time.
* **Secondary outcomes:** Degree of cervical dilation reached prior to procedure measured by diameter of Pratt dilator where loss of resistance first noticed, difficulty of additional dilation (if required), overall procedural difficulty, ability to complete the procedure on first attempt, patient acceptability (pain scores, adverse effects, preferences).
* **Other outcomes:** Side effects (pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, chills), immediate complications.

# YYYMethods

* Study design: randomised placebo control cross-over trial

* Study centre: Beijing Tongren Hospital, Beijing, China

* Study follow-up: 12 months (phase 1); further 12 months (phase 2)

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: 61 (28%) were excluded or lost to follow-up by 12 months

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean 9.6 ±1.68 years (range 6-12 years)

* Gender: 117 boys, 103 girls

* Culture: Chinese

* Inclusion criteria:

* aged 6-12 years
* SER −1.00 D to −6.00 D in both eyes
* astigmatism of ≤ −1.50 D both eyes
* distance BCVA 0.20 logMAR or better in both eyes
* IOP < 21 mm Hg
* Exclusion criteria:

* children with ocular diseases (eg, amblyopia, strabismus, corneal scar, cataract, glaucoma, or ocular tumour)
* previous or current treatment with atropine, pirenzepine, contact lenses, BFs, or PALs for myopia
* allergy to atropine, cyclopentolate, or excipients

# YYYInterventions

* 0.01% atropine eyedrops (n = 110)

* Placebo eyedrops (n = 110)

# YYYOutcomes

* Primary outcomes

* Change in SER from baseline (cycloplegic autorefractiobn)
* Change in AL from baseline (Haag Streit Lenstar LS900)
* Measurements taken at baseline 6 and 12 months (phase 1). In phase 2 placebo group crossed over to 0.01% atropine and the 0.01% atropine group crossed over to placebo to evaluate rebound

* Unit of analysis: child-based (right eye)

This means that the gluteus medius and minimus insertions onto the greater trochanter were partially divided anteriorly, leaving the posterior part of their insertions intact. The anterior capsule was divided and subsequently repaired prior to closure, followed by repair of the detached portion of the gluteal muscles."

The single divided tendon and posterior capsule were subsequently repaired with a transosseous repair to their initial position prior to closure. The insertions of the abductor muscles were left intact throughout the procedure."

# YYYMethods

Aim: non-inferiority & superiority, efficacy and safety
Design: parallel-group (phase III)
Blinding: double-blind, double-dummy; groups blinded: participants, outcome adjudicators
Study duration: February 2006 to January 2007
Duration of intervention: 10 to 14 days
Duration of follow-up: 30 to 35 days
Method of randomisation: no description was provided
Method of concealment of allocation: use of a central telephone system for allocation of participants
Primary efficacy analysis set: participants who: 1) received at least one dose of study medication, 2) un-
derwent planned surgery, 3) had a primary efficacy outcome that could be evaluated
Primary safety analysis set: participants who received at least one dose of study medication

Withdrawals: not reported
Exclusions: rivaroxaban group (430): 34 (2.7%) did not receive study drug, 19 (1.5%) did not undergo
the planned surgery, 376 (30%) had uninterpretable venography; enoxaparin group (399): 38 (3%) did
not receive study drug, 22 (1.7%) did not undergo the planned surgery, 339 (26.5%) had uninterpretable
venography

# YYYParticipants

Diagnosis: scheduled to TKA
Location of participants: 19 countries (Austria, Belgium, Canada, China, Colombia, Czech Republic,
Denmark, France, Germany, Israel, Italy, Mexico, the Netherlands, Norway, Peru, Poland, South Africa,
Spain, Sweden)
Number of participants randomised: 2531
Age (years; mean and range): (safety analysis population) rivaroxaban 67.6 (28 to 91); enoxaparin 67.6
(30 to 90)
Gender (male %): (safety analysis population) rivaroxaban 363 (29.8%); enoxaparin 418 (33.7%)
Baseline imbalances: the proportion of female participants was different between the groups (P = 0.03)
Inclusion criteria:

• 18 years of age or older and scheduled for TKA

Exclusion criteria:

•   Active bleeding or a high risk of bleeding that contraindicated the use of LMWH
•   Any contraindication to the use of enoxaparin or any condition necessitating adjustment of its dose
•   Conditions preventing bilateral venography
•   Clinically significant liver disease
•   Concomitant use of protease inhibitors of the human immunodeficiency virus or fibrinolytic agents
•   Planned IPC
•   Requirement of ongoing anticoagulant therapy
•   Pregnancy or breast-feeding

Concomitant interventions: none
Excluded interventions: none

Rivaroxaban group:
Intervention: rivaroxaban (oral) 10 mg once daily
Starting time: after surgery: 6 to 8 hours
Duration: 10 to 14 days

Enoxaparin group:

Starting time: before surgery: 12 hours
Duration: 10 to 14 days

characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Walking training Provided in addition to routine rehabilitation. This comprised: - Health education - assessment by designated rehabilitation therapist who assigns a training plan. Education of patient and family, including on assisting with rehabilitation training. - Seated balance training: "Sitting training can be implemented 48-72 hours after the patient's main vital signs are stable and the symptoms of the nervous system no longer progress. Ask the patient to sit up from the lateral position to the bedside, bend the neck and trunk sideways, use the Cao 2014 arm of the unaffected upper limb as a lever to hook the affected leg, and then move the legs to the bedside. Push the legs to facilitate the patient to sit up. For training, choose a bench with a height of 40 cm, which is conducive to a more stable landing of the lower limbs. Gradually make the patient transition from an unsupportive sitting position to a stationary sitting position that does not require support. Ask the patient to train. At the same time, adjust the posture by moving the center of gravity, and finally obtain the balance in the sitting position." - Standing balance training: "Getting the patient to stand as early as possible is usually the most ideal rehabilitation goal. During the training, the patient's feet can be moved back, the hips are bent, and the trunk is required to keep straight and forward, and then the back shoulders are moved forward over their toes and knees, the center of gravity reaches their feet, and then the body is forward and upward. stand up. During training, the upper and lower limbs on the affected side were immobilized with splints and supported externally. Avoid synergistic and antagonistic imbalances that lead to overstretching of muscle groups. Actively correct the resting alignment of the patient's joints to improve their functional position. Avoid knee flexion, fix a 1kg sandbag on the ankle of the affected limb to make it bear the weight, and the patient stands with the help of the walker with both hands. When in a standing position, the feet should be shoulder-width apart with the hips and knees extended, keeping the torso upright. Ask them to stand with weight and move their center of gravity back and forth to perform static and dynamic balance training." - Walking training: "Standing with weight and actively implementing walking training in the early stage is more likely to promote the recovery of trunk strength. In the early stage, post-weight-bearing walking training was carried out, 2 times a day, 10-15 minutes/time, and gradually extended to 45 minutes/time. During walking training, the splint should be fixed on the upper and lower limbs of the affected side, and a 1kg sandbag should be fixed on the ankle of the lower limb to make the affected leg bear weight, and it is easier to train the patient to stand. The trainer stands on the lateral side of the patient's affected side, and holds the patient's belt to control the patient to avoid falling injury. The patient was asked to first step the affected leg, extend the hip, and control the knee extension to prepare for the swing phase of the unaffected leg. If you have difficulty walking, you can be assisted by a trainer." - Stair training: "When the Brunstrom level of the patient's lower extremities exceeds level 3, the training of going up and down the stairs can be implemented, 2 times/day, 45 minutes/time. The trainer is located on the hemiplegic side behind the patient to assist him in completing the training. When going up the stairs, the affected leg should go up first, and when going down the stairs, the healthy leg should go down first. Actively encourage and praise patients for their progress and build confidence."

(2) Routine rehabilitation therapy

"The control group received routine rehabilitation therapy, including good limb placement and instructing family members to perform passive massage of the upper and lower limbs on the affected side."

title.S: Early response to antipsychotic drug therapy as a clinical marker of subsequent response in the treatment of schizophrenia

journal.S: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology

outcome.S: Response defined primarily as a 50% improvement in PANSS total score, with additional response thresholds also available; PANSS total-score change; depressive symptoms measured with MADRS; extrapyramidal symptoms including parkinsonism, akathisia, and dyskinesia; weight change and categorical weight gain; laboratory measures including triglycerides and prolactin; and adverse events. Remission, CGI-Severity, hospitalization, quality of life, functioning, subjective well-being, and cognition were measured but did not provide usable separate data for the randomized early-non-responder groups.

(1) Aerobic and resistance exercise

"The combined aerobic and resistance exercise group performed a 60-min combined exercise session three times a week for 16 wks."

"Each exercise intervention comprised a 5-min warm-up, a 10-min stretching exercise, a 20-min resistance exercise, a 20-min aerobic exercise, and a 5-min cool down (Table 1). Subjects performed standardized whole-body stretching and light walking during the warm-up and cool-down periods. The main stretching exercise included 10 stretching movements (shoulder flexion/extension, shoulder abduction/adduction, trunk flexion/extension, and hip flexion/extension, and hip abduction/adduction) with a 6-sec passive stretching, 3-sec muscular contractions, and a 2-sec relaxation. Aerobic exercise included a 10-min fast-walking on a sloping way and another 10 min walking in upstairs. Exercise intensity was established at 50% to 60% of heartrate reserve using the heart rate monitor system (RX800CX, Polar Finland) for 8 wks and then increased to 60% to 70% of heart rate reserve for the remaining 8 wks. Resistance exercise was carried out using elastic resistance bands. Subjects performed resistance exercise, which included lunges, squats, hip flexion/extension, hip abduction/adduction, knee flexion/extension, shoulder abduction/adduction, shoulder flexion/extension, and abdominal crunch/back extension. Exercise intensity was progressed from 10 to 15 repetitions with two to three sets for each motion for 8 wks, and the resistance levels of the elastic band was gradually increased for the remaining 8 wks. Resistance exercise was performed using a rating of perceived exertion of 11 to 16 (light to hard) using the Borg Scale. The exercise program was supervised by a trained exercise rehabilitation specialist and physical therapist."

(2) Control

"The control group received unsystematic physical activities or played Korean chess at the identical time. The control group did not receive any exercise intervention. They were asked to continue their normal daily activities. Most of them performed very light physical activities such as slow cycling with a cycle ergometer, walking on the hallway, or playing Korean chess."

# YYYMethods

Prospective randomised controlled single-centre clinical trial.

Exclusions after randomisation: none.

Losses of follow-up: 7 (in total from both groups; no additional information provided).

Period: December 2008 until January 2011.

Duration of follow-up: 24 months.

# YYYParticipants

Country: China.

Participants: 74 (test group, n = 45; control group, n = 29).

Age: mean 46 ± 24 years (between 18 and 70 years).

Sex: male 31 (42%) and female 43 (58%).

Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 70 years; new-onset DVT; the course of disease no longer than 14 days; complete patency of the major branch of the distal iliac vein after CDT with > 50% residual stenosis; signed informed consent.

Exclusion criteria: Contraindications to anticoagulation and thrombolysis: patients with severe renal impairment (Cr CL < 30 mL/min); patients in terminal stage of cancer with a life expectancy of < 3 months, and patients reporting previous or current use of thrombolytic procedures, including surgery and thrombolysis.

# YYYInterventions

Angioplasty or stenting: In the test group, balloon dilatation and stenting (diameter: 12–14 mm, length: 6–12 cm) were performed through the femoral vein, before the junction with the deep femoral vein, in all participants; residual stenosis < 10% was acceptable.

Control: Quote — “The patients in the control group were given the same treatment after the thrombolytic catheters were removed.” No stent was implanted in the control group.

Co-treatment: All participants underwent implantation of an inferior vena cava filter. A 4F Uni*fuse catheter was inserted into the deep vein of the affected extremity (femoral vein). No further details about puncture, such as ultrasound aid, were given. Urokinase (0.6 mg/d) was infused by a constant-rate pump. Following thrombolysis, intermittent deep vein venography was performed to determine residual stenosis. If it was > 50%, subjects were randomised. Average duration of postoperative urokinase infusion was 3–5 days, and total dosage was 1.0–3.5 mg. LMWH was simultaneously injected subcutaneously twice daily. Then, warfarin was given orally for anticoagulation until RNI 2-2.5 for at least 6 months (6-24 months). There was no mention of compression stocking therapy.

# YYYOutcomes

Patency of lower extremity deep vein, postoperative clinical efficacy (with VCSS and C in CEAP) and postoperative quality of life (CIVIQ), from baseline until 24 months.

PE and death were not analysed outcomes, but the study authors reported that no fatal PE or death occurred in the study (until 24 months). Adverse events (limb pain) reported at an intermediate time point.

characteristics_interventions.S:
(1) Exercise group (n = 15)

"The focus of the exercise was on physical activity and functional performance (based on the HIFE program), to improve the subjects' lower-limb strength, balance and gait ability. The program includes lower-limb strength (e.g. chair stand) and balance exercises (e.g. weight shifting outside support surface), standing (e.g. knee bend) and walking (e.g. obstacle crossing course)" Holmgren 2006

"The two daily training sessions were divided between exercise according to the HIFE program and implementing of the same in to everyday life activities, e.g. walking outdoors or sweep the yard. All exercises were performed at a high intensity, if possible, for each subject. 'High intensity' was defined as (i) strength exercises comprising at least two sets of exercises with 8 – 12 repetitions (maximum), (ii) the balance exercises were close to the subjects’ balance maximum, and (iii) the subject did not rest more than necessary, all according to the HIFE program"

"In addition, there was a 1-hour educational discussion session, per week. These discussions were about the increased risks of complications after stroke, such as falls. During the last week of intervention, an individualized home-based exercise program was designed by the physiotherapist. This home exercise program was part of the intervention program and consisted of a maximum of three different exercises that were based on the exercises performed during the 5-week intervention. It was easy to adjust the intensity of all the exercises so that they could be modified as the subject progressed. The instructions were to perform this home-based exercise program three times a week at least until the 3-month follow-up"

Length of intervention period: 5 weeks. In addition, participants were instructed to continue to perform the home-based exercise programme 3 times a week at least until the 3-month follow-up.

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "the exercise sessions, which lasted approximately 45 min each, were performed six times each week, a total of 30 exercise sessions over 5 weeks. Subjects also received a 45-min session per day of activities related to real-life situations. In addition, one day each week there was a 1-hour educational discussion session, a total of five educational sessions over 5 weeks"

Intervention provider: physiotherapist and occupational therapist

(2) Control group (n = 19) Education only

"The group discussions were about communication difficulties, fatigue, depressive symptoms, mood swings, personality changes and dysphagia, all more or less hidden dysfunctions after stroke and how to cope with these difficulties. There was no special focus on the risks of falling in these discussions"

Length of intervention period: 5 weeks

Number of sessions and length of individual sessions: "met once a week for 1 hour of educational session"

Intervention provider: occupational therapist

characteristics_markdown.S:
# YYYMethods

* Study design: parallel-group RCT

* Study centre: single (Tianjin Eye Hospital Optometric Center, China)

* Number randomized: 421 children (3 excluded prior to randomisation)

* Study follow-up: 24 months

* Exclusions and losses to follow-up: 3 lost to follow-up

# YYYParticipants

* Age: mean = 8.13 (SD 1.0) years

* Gender: 212 boys, 209 girls

* Culture: Chinese

* Inclusion criteria:

* Chinese schoolchildren aged 6 to 12 years old who had mild to moderate myopia, defined as objective spherical equivalence (SE) and binocular astigmatism between −1.00 to −6.00 D, and astigmatism ≤ 1.50 D
* reduced vision in a recent school health examination
* corrected visual acuity less than 1.0
* normal intraocular pressure
* children who could undergo follow-up examinations following the study protocol
* children from whom written informed consent to participate in the study could be obtained
* children capable of undergoing cycloplegia
* Exclusion criteria:

* abnormal binocular function, amblyopia, or manifest strabismus, changes in objective spherical equivalent in both eyes as measured by cycloplegic and non-cycloplegic refraction of less than 1.00 D
* children with ocular diseases other than myopia, and children with ocular or systemic diseases that may affect myopia or refractive power
* allergic to atropine, cyclopentolate, or benzalkonium chloride
* wearing contact lenses, bifocal lenses, or progressive lenses throughout the trial period

# YYYInterventions

* 0.05% atropine eye drops, dosed once nightly in both eyes (n=212)

* Placebo (sodium citrate) eye drops, dosed once nightly in both eyes (n=209)

# YYYOutcomes

* Primary outcome

* Change in spherical equivalent cycloplegic autorefraction
* Secondary outcome

* Change in AL as measured by non contact partial coherence interferometry in the study eye
* Measurements taken at 12, 28 and 24 months

* Unit of analysis: eye-based "The differences between biometric parameters and baseline at each time point were calculated for both eyes." "The differences between biometric parameters and baseline at each time point were calculated for both eyes. Missing data values were imputed based on the breakdown of other variables in the dataset. P-values were generated from generalized estimating equations with specified standard errors to adjust for correlations and compare multiple eyes."

# YYYRisk of Bias

| Bias domain | Authors’ judgement | Support for judgement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Randomisation process** | Low risk of bias | A permutation block approach, stratified by age and sex, will be used to randomly allocate each location (block size: 4, ratio: 1:1). A contracted professional research body, Medical Edge Ltd, will prepare and maintain the mapping table.' No suggestion of a problem with randomisation process (see Table 1 p4). |
| **Deviations from intended interventions** | Low risk of bias | The identification of research-specific medications were blinded to researchers, children, and their caretakers. ITT analysis performed. |
| **Missing outcome data** | Low risk of bias | Data available for 95.3% of intervention group and 90.5% of placebo group. |
| **Measurement of the outcome** | Low risk of bias | Appropriate measurement methods were used. Measurements same for all participants. Outcome assessors were masked. |
| **Selection of the reported results** | Some concerns | No Statistical Management Plan available to judge this outcome. |
| **Overall** | Some concerns | The study is judged to raise some concerns in at least one domain for this result, but not to be at high risk of bias for any domain. |

characteristics_interventions.S:
## General details

* **Surgeon:** One surgeon with more than 10 years experience performed all cases

* **Components:** Hydroxyapatite-coated or titanium-coated non-cemented stems with bipolar cups

* **anaesthesia:** All surgeries were performed within 48h after injury

* **Care protocol:** Tranexamic acid administered during surgery. Three doses of intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis (cefuroxime) given: 0, 12 and 24 h after surgery. Prophylactic dose of LMWH (low molecular weight heparin) was provided for the postoperative 30 days. Standard postoperative opioid sparing pain-management protocol. Post op full weightbearing, therapy started within 12 h after surgery. Criteria of discharge involved the ability to get out of bed and to use the toilet independently and to walk safely with aids.

## Intervention group 1 (Lateral)

Anterolateral approach

"Briefly, the anterolateral approach (ALA) is performed on standard operation table, by incising the fascia lata and dissecting the distal part of adductor muscles."

## Intervention group 2 (Anterior)

Minimally invasive direct approach

"patients were in supine position on a special fracture table. The skin incision starts 3–3 cm lateral and distal from the ASIS towards the fibular head, varies from 8 to 12 cm in length, depending on the shape of the body. The fascia is incised above the muscle and the approach develops medially into the interval between the sartorius muscle and fascia lata; the circumflex femoral artery branches are coagulated and Hohmann retractors are placed superior and inferior to femoral neck and to the anterior acetabulum. Following excision of the anterior capsule and oscillation through neck, the femoral head is removed and the prosthesis head is measured and probed. Then, the leg is hyperextended in 120 ° of external rotation. In this position of the knee, the intercondylar external rotation of femur is set to 90 °; the extremity is positioned in 30–40 ° of hyperextension and in 20 ° of adduction. By the specially designed Hohmann-retractors, the proximal femur is elevated and the femoral part is prepared."
